That this House calls upon the Government to immediately bring in stimulative proposals to reduce unemployment by a minimum of 2.5 per cent within the next 12 months, given the failure of the Government to live up to its commitment to make job creation its number one priority, and its pursuit, instead, of a policy of cutbacks which has led to a rise in unemployment in three of the last four months.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be able to move this Opposition Day motion today. It is particularly fine to do so with the kind of billing which was given to it yesterday by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). In answer to a question by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the Prime Minister said the following:
-1 suppose if the Hon. Member had a formula, or the Leader of the Opposition, or anyone else, that he could give me, whereby we can bring down unemployment by 2.5 per cent in the next month or two, I would grab it and say thank you, and I know the country would too.
Last week the Action Group of the New Democratic Party, after completing a tour across the country and talking with over 400 groups and individuals, released to the public a plan or an approach. I certainly cannot promise people here or people in the country that this approach would reduce the unemployment rate by 2.5 per cent in a month or two, but it would certainly give the country the kind of direction which, over the next year, would take our unemployment rate from the present unacceptable, humanly tragic level of 11.2 per cent down by that 2.5 per cent about which we talked yesterday in the House of Commons. That is a commitment which I think the people of Canada are demanding. It is a commitment which they feel is urgent and crucial, a commitment which they feel is only just, given the promises and the positions taken by the Government and the present Prime Minister prior to his election.
What we have in Canada is a crisis for people. I want to commence my remarks this morning by talking about some of the people I met across the country in the national tour which our Action Group organized to reach out to communities across Canada. There were some tragic stories which pointed out in a deeply emotional way to me the sense of human loss
that we as a country are experiencing because of the existing tragic unemployment figures.
For instance, I want to talk about a man named Robert MacDonald in Cape Breton who has spent over 18 months criss-crossing the country putting in applications to company after company and not succeeding in finding a position. I want to talk about the unemployed construction workers who met us en masse in Edmonton and conveyed to us, in their anger and in their concern, their own outrage at unemployment rates of 75 per cent to 80 per cent in some of the particular skills which they represented in that city. I want to talk about the unemployed textile workers, most of whom were women 50 years to 55 years of age. They met us in Montreal. These women told us that their lives had lost meaning, that their capacity to provide for the needs of their families had been stripped away from them, and that their own sense of pride in the country was being sapped by the cruel way in which they were being treated as middle-aged unemployed women.
I want to talk about a young man, Pierre Desjardins in Moncton, who indicated to us that this was the year of the youth, yet those who come out of university in Moncton face unemployment rather than the prospect of jobs. I want to talk about Ron and Tony Camponi, Metis leaders in Saskatoon. They told me about the 200 units of Metis housing produced in Saskatoon for which Metis construction workers could not even bid in the last three years.
I want to talk about young people like Terry Bellavance who spoke to us in Thunder Bay on behalf of the Ontario March of Dimes. He is one of the many disabled or handicapped people in the country. He is looking for a chance to play a fair role in this community, a chance to live the life to which every Canadian is entitled.
I do not want to talk only about the human tragedy because the most exciting part of this tour or the most exciting part of this experience was for me to hear from people across the country that they felt this was not a tragedy which was unavoidable. It is not a tragedy that we simply have to accept. It is something that it is possible, by action, direction and leadership, to do something about. The people from whom I want to bring the message to this House of Commons are people like the woman named Core Strandberg of Vancouver who sat down with us and spent an afternoon talking in detail about the economic development corporations springing up across British Columbia, 36 of them in total. She showed a kind of grassroots dynamism and potential that we have to support and encourage.

1 want to talk to you about women like Laurilie Kilgour of Hamilton who, despite discouragement and her difficulty as a woman in getting financing from our banking system, started a small graphics factory. She built it up into a thriving small business, providing employment within that community. She built it up despite the Government rather than with the support and encouragement of the Government.
I want to talk to you about people like Richard Cashin of St. John's and Jack Nichol in British Columbia who told us about the vast potential that is there if we build on our fish resources on both coasts of this country. 1 want to talk to you about people like Rick Fuerth from the Essex County Federation of Agriculture in my constituency. He told us in detail about the jobs that are there if we in this country give the kind of support to agriculture, one of our key resource sectors, that it deserves.
I want to talk to you about people like the young man from the unemployed Action Centre in Thunder Bay. He came before us and said that here in Thunder Bay just down the road is a shipyard that used to produce new ships. He said it used to provide thousands of jobs, but now does not do so because we have let the shipping industry in this country disappear. We have not given it the kind of support and encouragement that the jobs of Canadian people demand and deserve.
I want to talk to you about the Federation of New Brunswick Woodlot Owners, small owners who came to us and said that if we gave them the support instead of giving it to the large forest companies, they would reforest this, province and they would do it by providing extra jobs as well. I want to talk to you about groups like the Mining Association of Canada who came to us and talked with excitement about the potential that is there for taking the new technology in this country, marrying it together with the tremendous resource base and the mineral sector that we have, and turning us into a country that can produce the mining equipment that a country as rich in resources as this country is deserves to be producing.
The ideas are there, the potential is there and the capacity is there. What is needed is a sense of will, a sense of leadership to realize this potential. In the report we put out last week, we attempted to provide that sense of direction and leadership. We did so around three broad themes because we think there is an answer that can focus on three broad directions of change.
The first is a community self-direction, a philosophy that says, let's give support and encouragement to these hundreds and hundreds of community development organizations, cooperatives, small business organizations, and municipal Governments that want to take the potential that is there at the community level and turn it into jobs. They gave us detailed recommendations and ideas to do so. We have included those recommendations within our report. I recommend them to the Government. They are not designed to embarrass or score partisan points, but to put across the message from Canadians that they believe something can be done in this country and
that they have serious ideas to suggest. These are ideas we have summed up around the notions of how to encourage and open up the potential for community co-operatives, how to assist economic development corporations throughout the country, how to find detailed ways to give real help to small business, and how to give assistance to municipal Governments so that they can do what the Federation of Canadian Municipalities has said is crucial, and that is, to rebuild the infrastructure in this country. However, in order to achieve this, it takes more than simply saying, "Let 100 flowers bloom". We cannot simply say that we will encourage all of these things to take place.
As well, we need to have a sense of national self-direction. We need to have a philosophy indicating that to achieve this kind of community self-direction, we need a sense at the national level of corporate accountability. We need a commitment from the large-scale corporate sector to pay its fair share of taxation, to take its proper role in the training needs of the country, and to give us an indication of a sense of responsibility to communities so that when a large corporation wants to shut down a plant, it talks with the community and gives it a chance to develop some kind of alternative by having workers take it over or by having a local economic development corporation take it over.
There must be as well a sense of independence in our interest rate policy. There must be a serious effort to build on our resources. We have to practise a structure of fair trade rather than throw ourselves at the mercy of the rest of the world with the kind of free trade philosophy that does not recognize how tough and harsh the international economy actually is.
Besides this sense of community self-direction and national self-direction, we need a profound commitment to equity and equality in the workplace. Across the country, we have not given that equity and equality to the women who make up half of our workforce, to the disabled who rightly demand their fair share of the benefits we in this country have to offer, to visible minorities and to those who represent ethnocultural communities. There has to be a sense of equity established through aggressive action, which frankly must be more aggressive than the action the Minister has yet taken.
That is the kind of broad direction that we see possible. It is a direction that we have described in something like 70 recommendations. However, we must take the first step now. We need a Budget that takes that first step now. In six weeks' time, we can have a Budget that puts jobs first. We can have a Budget that makes serious moves toward cutting our unemployment rate by 2.5 per cent and giving us the 300,000 extra jobs that would be necessary to do that.
We have to stop playing Chicken Little over the deficit. The deficit is an important concern. We in this Party have always recognized that. However, if we rush around the country saying that the sky is falling and we have to worry about the
April 16, 1985

deficit, we will not get the jobs this country needs and, just as ironically, we will not get the deficit down.
When this kind of preaching started in this country in 1975, the deficit was $3 billion. There has been Budget after Budget which has told us that we must be concerned about the deficit and that we must bring it down. As that has happened year by year, we have seen the deficit rise to $36 billion. I predict now, as I have predicted before, that if we have a Budget that concentrates on cut-backs and reducing the deficit, it will result a year from now in fewer jobs and a higher deficit than we presently have. The only way to get the deficit down over the next three to five years is to take the kind of approach which we are talking about in our counter-Budget that will put stimulus into the economy and get Canada growing once more. We have laid out a budget plan which is based on shifts within the Budget, shifts of expenditure and shifts of taxation, shifts which will bring us an extra 4.2 billion in spending, $3.1 billion on community development, and $1.1 billion on resource upgrading. It would shift $2.7 billion of tax breaks from the commitment to the corporate tax sector and the wealthy to a commitment to tax breaks for the working people. Another $2.7 billion can be saved in interest rate reductions and in reducing the rate of unemployment.
To succeed in this new direction we need a different approach. We need to give real help to small businesses and communities, not the Conservative Government's give-aways to large oil companies and the Commercial Bank of Canada. We need a real priority for jobs, not the Conservative Government's paralysis over cut-backs and deficits. We need real moves to build our resources, not the Conservative Government's delays on reforestation and its dismal record on agriculture. We need real efforts to build on our industrial base through fair trade, not the Conservative Government's sense of sell-out that free trade and "Warehouse Canada" represent. We need a Government that means what it says. We need a Government that comes through with the promise and the commitment to make jobs a priority. We need a Government that Canadians will not have to say is a mean-spirited Government which wants to run on the backs of the unemployed by way of changes such as the severance pay and retirement points which the Minister will bring in. In doing those things it will shift the problems of the economy on the backs of the people who deserve to suffer the least.
There is, as the Prime Minister asked us yesterday, an approach, a path, and a plan which would cut the unemployment rate by 2.5 per cent. I urge the Government to follow that direction, not the dismal and sorry direction in which it has begun.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to say that I very much welcome this opportunity to respond on behalf of the Government to the motion which has been put before the House today by the New Democratic Party. It gives me an opportunity to comment on what the Government is doing-a record which I feel is very substantial for a period of six months. It also gives me an opportunity to comment on the recommendations that were brought forward by the Task Force on Unemployment which was set up by the New Democratic Party.
I found the report interesting. I want to tell the Hon. Member that I gave him and his colleagues the courtesy of reading through it. I did not examine it all in detail but I did look at it. I want to say that I think it was a good effort on their part and I think it was an important thing to do, that is, to go out and consult with people across the country on this very important issue. I know because that is what I have been doing for the last number of months.
Certainly, trying to come to grips with this issue can only be done at the local level. I think that both the people in government and those who are on the New Democratic Party task force have tried to do that. It has not yet dawned on the Hon. Members of the Liberal Party that that approach is one they also should be taking, but perhaps having read the two reports of the two Parties, they will begin to think about getting jobs for people other than all those Liberal candidates who were defeated last autumn.
I would like to comment on whether or not this Canada unlimited project, which promises to solve all the problems of unemployment, is really going to be able to do that. What I found when I first saw the results in the newspaper reports was the tone, the things which had been discovered and, in fact, the reversal of New Democratic policy in the field of job-creation, unemployment and training. The first headline I saw read, "NDP Thrust would put Job Funds into Community Hands". Abandoning the big centralized machine of former years, that is the way it would go.
Seven or eight years ago.

Well, if the Hon. Member would look at the Government's labour market strategy and at the various programs which have already been put in place, he would find that community based plans are indeed the thrust of the Government's undertakings. The next headline I saw in the newspapers read, "NDP Proposes Job-Creation Without Big Deficit Increase". Surely, Sir, that is a real change of mind for those hon. members of the New Democratic Party. I welcome what they have to say. I know, as well as my colleagues, that we have to stimulate job-creation, create more jobs, but at the same time we have to be very fearful of adding to the weight of a deficit.
The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) is quoted as saying, "We simply can't accept that we have large

deficits continuing. It doesn't make any sense". We have been trying to tell the New Democratic Party that for some time. Of course, it does not make any sense, and I am glad to see in that Party's report a recognition of the things which should be done. The Hon. Member talked about corporate accountability, bringing in the private sector. The whole plan which has been outlined in the last few months, in moving away from the short-term job-creation dead-end which used to be in effect, is to bring in the co-operation of the provinces and the private sector. Certainly there should be more contribution by the private sector and what we are already doing is taking that into account.
It seems to me, Sir, that these things are in the report which 1 read and which I welcome because I think there is a dawning of a new light in the New Democratic Party. I think it shows that, having gone out and consulted with the people of Canada, those Hon. Members now realize where action must be taken, what people want and how it can best be incorporated. As a result of that, I expect the wholehearted support of the New Democratic Party for the steps the Government is taking in this regard. Who knows, the New Democratic Party may even recover somewhat from that 17 per cent if it pursues these very sensible methods.
Not much, though.

My colleague says, "Not much", but we will look at it over the months. Unfortunately, even though the NDP has presented some interesting proposals, not terrifically original but some ideas in the field of job-creation, it cannot wean itself completely away from thinking that there has to be a sudden cure of all ills by Government and that it is going to happen overnight. Those Hon. Members still have the feeling that somehow you can utter a few sentences and total unemployment, total deficits and the total difficulties we are facing will be eradicated. I suppose they take that approach because that is part of their long-term thinking. They cannot move away from it because, of course, they do not face the reality of day-to-day Government. They can indulge in euphoric thinking. From time to time Members indulge in this business of sitting and thinking about what can be done in the abstract. They realize they will not have to put some of these grandiose schemes into practice. Indeed, with 17 per cent of the electorate supporting them, why should they think that way? It is not likely that they will have to take on those responsibilities very soon. But we do have to take on those responsibilities and we have to consider all the factors.
We, Mr. Speaker, have to consider the deficit. We have to consider interest rates. We have to consider industrial investment policy, world trade, tax reform, energy policy, labour market development and much, much more. We have to deal with these issues, and we are. As my colleagues will know, we are dealing with them in the new energy agreements on both the East Coast and the West Coast. Governments have struggled for years to obtain these energy agreements, but we have
accomplished it and the agreements will generate new wealth and create new jobs.
We are dealing with these issues through measures to improve the environment. We are dealing with them through the control of Government waste. We are dealing with them in a taxpayers' Bill of Rights. Not least of all, we are dealing with them in a new labour market strategy which was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in February of this year. As the NDP has discovered in its trip across the country, that strategy is dealing with these issues. It is working with Canadians at the community level, with other Governments, labour organizations, and businesses large and small. For the first time this strategy is based on multi-year fundings so that one can begin to plan ahead. It reflects the regional diversity of this country and allows training, job creation and human resource development to go ahead according to the needs of the various parts of this country.
I ask you to look at the commitments we have already made, Sir; some $80 million over and above previous commitments for skills investment to help retrain that 46 year old warehouseman or the middle-aged woman whose job is being phased out, to help them retrain before they actually lose their jobs. That is a commitment which has not been made before and one we think we should be moving into with the help of business and other Governments.
There is $350 million for job development over and above what had been committed before. Any one of us in this House, no matter from what Party, who has seen or met or talked with someone who has been unemployed for long, recognizes his or her plight and knows that something has to be done about it so that a person does not face a lifetime without work. This money has been committed to create long-term jobs in concert with the provinces and private sector, jobs of a substantive nature rather than the short-term dead-end projects of the past.
There is $125 million for job entry to help young people entering the workforce for the first time to bridge the gap and make the transition from school to work with on-site experience. The same applies to women coming into the labour force for the first time, or perhaps re-entering the labour force after having been absent for a while. This program will help them to get into real jobs which will provide security and a future.
Just as we want individuals to have these opportunities, Sir, we want communities to have them as well. That is why we have earmarked $40 million to community futures, to look at communities which are in decline or where their industry could be in decline and ask what should be done beforehand to turn that situation around. I may say that I appreciate hearing from the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) who was up in Labrador and did a study of some of the communities there. He sent me a copy of that section of the report. I thank him for sending it to me because I know that we have the same interests at heart in trying to avoid the catastrophe which can happen to single industry towns and the people who live in them.
April 16, 1985

Sir, these measures in this new labour strategy indicate that this Government is taking a new approach with a new openness, a new and imaginative development of human resources and job creation while recognizing regional disparity. That is why we have earmarked $100 million for innovation and experimentation in this field. We look to Canadians to provide the creativity and ingenuity that they have to help in the search for answers. I have already talked with people, groups and organizations; people in organized labour, women's groups, people from the private sector and provincial Governments. I have asked them to come forward with ideas or pilot projects to see how we can move into this new world of work; to see that the experimental projects which prove successful can be utilized in other parts of the country.
It is the first time a Government has earmarked $100 million for innovation and I know, from talking with such organizations as the CLC, that they will be coming to us with their suggestions on how this money can be utilized. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because when this strategy was introduced at the First Ministers' Conference in Regina, among other people who happened to comment on it was the Minister responsible for economic security in Manitoba, Mr. Evans, and he said, "It is a move in the right direction". The Premier of Manitoba, Mr. Pawley, commented very favourably on the way in which the labour market strategy was developing, and indeed put his Government's approval on it.
I mention that because I think this is something we all have to work at. 1 do not think any single Government or any single sector can resolve this issue on its own. That is why we have sought opportunities to create permanent jobs for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. Opportunities! It is a key word, Sir, but central to those opportunities is another thing which I have enunciated here in the House which is being worked on at present and which Hon. Members will shortly be able to support when legislation is brought before the House. I am talking about the principle of employment equity, because that is central to any labour market strategy. We are determined that, once and for all, women, disabled persons, native people, and visible minorities will get the opportunities they should have in Canada's workforce in the market-place. They should do so as equal partners, having the same opportunity as anyone else. This in itself is a breakthrough. The Hon. Member may not believe so, but I can tell him that in the House of Commons it is a breakthrough.
We have gone further than this. I was pleased to announce last month that we are establishing a new code of conduct that will ensure employment equity in the Public Service and that will lead to a concept that we all endorse, the implementation of equal pay for work of equal value. These steps will lead to meaningful jobs for Canadians for ongoing periods. We have to establish solid and good foundations. That is what this new labour market strategy is attempting to do. We are optimistic about it.

I was glad that the NDP went across the country and discovered that the country is optimistic and there is confidence. I feel that there is very much confidence. I have just returned from a meeting of OECD countries in Italy on employment and technology. I was struck by the pessimism which abounds on this issue in many of the European countries as shown through their Governments. That same lack of confidence does not exist here in Canada. It does not exist because the people of Canada themselves are confident about the future. The Government has been stimulating that confidence in the market-place.
Some headlines in the press which indicate this confidence include one in the Montreal Gazette which reads: "Employment Outlook Best In Years, Survey Finds". The Toronto Globe and Mail said: "Prospects for Jobless Appear Brighter". The Telegraph Journal of Saint John, New Brunswick carried a headline which reads: "Summer-Job Situation Looks Bright". A headline in The Ottawa Citizen reads: "Job Outlook Improving StatsCan". In The Toronto Star one headline reads: "Small Firms Seen Creating 200,000 Jobs in Half a Year".
There is confidence in the country that this very great issue can be tackled, Mr. Speaker. There is confidence and there is a response. The Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) has set the tone for the NDP in criticizing the Challenge '85 program for students. As negative as he has been, and as much as he has tried to undermine that program and do away with jobs for young people this summer, 150,000 new jobs have been submitted, and the private sector itself has added an additional 50,000 jobs. It has added just under $100 million to a government established fund of $205 million. That fund has gone from $200 million to $300 million. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville is still trying to run it down and undermine it. That is a rather discouraging thing for young people.
Where are the jobs?

These people ask, "Where are the jobs?" They do not want young people to have jobs this summer. That is their whole approach. The difference between the New Democratic Party, the Liberal Party, whose Members do not take this issue up, and the Conservative Party is that we have faith in the people of Canada. We have faith that we will be able to bring unemployment down. We know that new jobs are there and are being created. We know that the new labour market strategy which is now under way is stimulating the people, the businesses, and the Governments of the country to create the jobs and the wealth that is necessary. That, Sir, is triggering our economic renewal.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a question relating to her reference to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I would like to ask her what action she has taken due to the many representations made on behalf of the 210 fishermen in Bonavista Bay. The Minister received a telex

from the Premier of Newfoundland, the Minister of Fisheries, and the Minister of Social Development some three or four months ago. Does the Minister remember the case of the 210 fishermen who had been judged as having had over-payments in unemployment insurance?
I know exactly what you are talking about. Go right ahead.

I just want to point out to the Minister, in a reference to unemployment insurance, the danger of the Minister and the Government giving a signal to the Unemployment Insurance Commission and employment offices across the country with regard to unemployment insurance in those particular offices.
When unemployment insurance benefits are examined, in the case of fish companies, you may find that an unemployment insurance stamp was given for two weeks when there was legally only one shipment on the books. When the audit is done it may said that that fisherman did not deserve those two weeks of unemployment insurance, although he did in 1982 or 1983, as most of these audits are determining. The fact of the matter is that those groups of fishermen and workers are judged to be guilty of an over-payment from the Commission and they have to pay back thousands of dollars.
In the case of the 210 fishermen in Bonavista Bay the Government of Newfoundland made a request for the Minister to intervene and to try to overlook the problem with these 210 workers. Can the Minister report to the House? Has she got her book with her that she can perhaps look at? Does she know of the 210 fishermen in Bonavista Bay that I am talking about?

I am quite familiar with Bonavista Bay. The Hon. Member will know that. He will also know that in the case he raises the mistake was made by the company concerned. I think he will understand that. He will also know that every person involved has a right to appeal. The Commission has notified every individual to file an appeal in this case. Any claims for repayment have been held up pending those appeals.

Mr. Speaker, 1 enjoyed the Minister's speech. As always, her heart is in the right place. It is her head and, unfortunately, her partisanship that gets her into trouble. There is a certain potential to deal with substance that she demonstrated in her speech. It is unfortunate that she found it necessary to launch cheap shots at my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), at the end of her otherwise fairly civilized discourse.
Oh, oh!

Unfortunately, civilized discourse is not Party commitment. Our quarrel is not with this Minister. This Minister is not the Mr. Scrooge or the Chicken Little of the Government running around saying that the sky is falling. The Minister who deserves that title is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). As this Minister knows, he is the one who has
been giving her trouble and making it difficult for her to do the things she has been talking about.
We have magnificent ideas and plans that the Minister has talked about. I have to ask her why only $40 million, why only $80 million? Why the small sums of money for what are excellent ideas? I know the answer. The answer has to do with the Scrooge-like quality of the people who run this Government.
I have a set of questions for the Minister. Since she has said she has had a chance to read our report, let me ask her if in Cabinet she will advocate the $2.7 billion in tax breaks that we recommend for middle and lower income people? Will she advocate $850 million for a community development fund? Will she advocate the proposal of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities for a $12 billion ten-year program to upgrade municipal infrastructure? Will she advocate a technology fund of $200 million a year? Will she accept the commitment to reforestation, the commitment to fisheries, and the commitment to agriculture? Will she see to it that her Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) puts that into effect? Will she see to it that new tax sources that could be tapped by asking corporations to make the very simple step of paying interest on deferred taxes are tapped? Will she accept the proposal that we raise taxes for upper income people to the fair levels that were there under Mr. MacEachen in the past? Will she, in short, make the kind of rhetorical commitment which she and her Party are so magnificent in making and try to translate it into real action instead of empty phrases? Will she see to it that we get real help for small business community development instead of seeing that $1.5 billion goes to the multinational oil companies and $60 billion to the Canadian Commercial Bank? Will the Minister put her own career on the line, her own commitment to fight in Cabinet for a serious "jobs first" Budget? If so, she will have my support.

Mr. Speaker, I have to tell the Hon. Member that I have been putting my political career on the line every day since 1972, and I can tell him that the people in my district seem to feel that the way I have been doing that has merited their support. I hope I can continue to do that.
Hear, hear!

I must say I listened to the questions that have been posed by the Hon. Member. But what happens is that he then blows his case. I know that in his comments on his report he said that we have to be concerned about the deficit. There was a recognition that the size of the deficit has its dangers. But then the Hon. Member turned around and posed questions to me such as: Would I add $12 billion to the expenditures here, and add some other billions there? I have to tell the Hon. Member that he cannot have it both ways.
Of course you can.

That is what the whole story is about. There can be a proper basis for a labour market strategy, and
April 16, 1985

on that you build, but you do not try to resolve things only by throwing money at them. You try to accomplish this by developing human resources. I have to tell the Hon. Member that of all the Ministers in this Cabinet, there is no one who has received better treatment from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) than I have. There is no one else who can show that in the last few months he or she has received $900 million from him. That is not a bad beginning.
The rest of them were a bunch of slackers. That is the problem. I agree they are not pushing enough.

And so, Mr. Speaker, I just mentioned that that $900 million is going into all sorts of measures which I tried to outline and which are going to be very beneficial. Starting now with the summer program, they are allowing people to train and equip themselves for the jobs and the work in the future.

The period for questions and comments is now terminated. I would like to recognize the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand).
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, I want to start by saying that we fully support the motion before the House. We believe that stimulus is necessary to deal with the unemployment situation, that goals are necessary, and that priorities are necessary. I want to say right away that we along with the Party that presented the motion do not believe the Government's approach is working. We do not think the approach will work and we feel that the Government has not lived up to the promises made during the election campaign.
With respect to this very important issue, I refer to a Gallup poll published on January 28, 1985. It reported that 56 per cent of Canadians believe that unemployment is still Canada's major problem. That is correct, of course, and if we look at the figures, Mr. Speaker, we will see why.
In January, 1984, last year, when the Liberals were in power and we were coming out of the recession, the rate of unemployment was 11.4 per cent. In June of last year the unemployment rate went down to 11.2 per cent. It hit a low in the middle of the summer, in July, of 11 per cent, and then in September, the month when the Conservative Government was
Supply
elected, the unemployment rate went up to 11.6 per cent. It has been around that level since then.
Not less than last year at this time.

In October, the unemployment rate was 11.2 per cent, in November, it was 11.3 per cent, in January, it was 11.2 per cent, in February, it was 11.0 per cent and in March, it was 11.2 per cent.
As you can see from the figures, Mr. Speaker, there is relatively little change in the unemployment figures over the last year. Let us look at the averages in the year's preceding
1984.	In 1979, the average unemployment rate was 7.4 per cent, in 1980, it was 7.5 per cent, in 1981, it was 7.5 per cent, and then the rate jumped to 11 per cent in 1982 with the recession which hit the entire western developed world. That rate has stayed around 11 per cent since 1982, hitting its worst year in 1983 in the pit of the recession.
The Government had said over and over that once it was elected great confidence would be restored in the country, that businessmen would invest, that employment would climb and that unemployment would decline. As I pointed out, the figures do not show that. Not only do the figures not show that, but I want to use a tactic that was used very well by the Minister herself and also by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) who likes to quote headlines from newspapers.
I have here a Canadian Press story published in the Gazette dated October 5, 1984. It reads, "Economists forecast slowdown in Canada". That is from the Conference Board of Canada. A Gallup Poll of January 7, 1985 reports that fewer today expect unemployment to fall. Fewer expect unemployment to fall, that is the Conference Board's confidence in the Conservative Government which was supposed to instil all sorts of confidence. A story in The Globe and Mail, the great Conservative newspaper, dated December 5, reads, "Production and Employment drop sharply". On January 7, 1985, also from The Globe and Mail a headline reads, "Forty-two per cent expect increase in jobless in 1985". From March 26,
1985,	we have a Canadian Press story which is headed, "Most forecasters expect high unemployment in 1986".
The confidence which was supposed to return to Canada with the election of this Government, as was promised, is not there. It is not there as shown in the Gallup polls. It is not there as indicated by economists who analyse the situation. The Government's approach is not working and will not work. We need stimulus, but the Government is giving us cuts as exemplified in the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on November 8. In fact, it is withdrawing stimulus from the Canadian labour market rather than increasing it.
As I said, two things are necessary-we should have stimulus and we should have goals. Yesterday I was pleased when the Leader of the New Democratic Party rose in the House and asked whether we could have a six and five program for unemployment. I have been saying that myself for several years now. As a matter of fact, in the report of the task force

April 16, 1985
Supply
on employment opportunities published in 1981, we recommended a full employment policy. I am pleased to say that Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party supported that recommendation for a full employment policy, but the two Conservative Members on the committee dissented from that recommendation.
It is important to indicate that every time Governments in this country have fixed exact goals for unemployment, they have come close to attaining those goals. As was pointed out yesterday, under the six and five program for inflation, by setting those goals over a three-year period-and other factors came into play-inflation came down from approximately 13 per cent to less than 5 per cent because that was made a priority and it was a goal.
Let us look at the two other times since the Second World War when the Government of this country made full employment its goal and came very close to achieving it. In 1945, right after the war, the Liberal Government of Canada published a white paper on full employment. It set out goals to achieve full employment and the means of doing so. In the period from 1946 to 1953, the average rate of unemployment was 3 per cent. The next time a goal was set for full employment was when the Liberal Government set up the Economic Council of Canada in 1963. In its first report of 1964, it recommended a full employment policy. Immediately following that time, in the period from 1965 to 1967, the rate of unemployment was 3.8 per cent. We can see that when we set goals, as we did with the six and five for inflation and as we did in 1946 and 1964 for employment, we come close to achieving them because those goals are priorities and those priorities prevail over all other matters which come before the Government.
When I say that stimulus is necessary, of course I do not mean any kind of stimulus. I mean a well thought out and appropriate stimulus, a stimulus which is appropriate to our geography, population, resources, trading partners, and to the fact that we live next to the United States and so on. It must be a well balanced stimulus policy. It must be done in consultation and in co-operation with private business, trade unions, consumers' groups and so on.
Furthermore, we cannot continually look to the United States for programs to borrow. Canada is not the United States. As a matter of fact, if we were to judge Canada on economic bases alone, Canada would not exist. If we simply decided whether Canada was worth-while in economic terms, we would decide that it would not be, that we should join the United States; we would probably be better off economically if we were part of the United States. However, long ago, in 1867 and before, we decided for political reasons that we did not want to be Americans. We decided that we wanted to pay the political price to be Canadians which, as all of us know in the House, requires subsidies, cross-subsidies, building national railways, the CBC and airlines, to bring together the thin ribbon of population which extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That is Canada, that very thin ribbon of population of about 25 million people living next to one of the largest and
most powerful countries in the world. We cannot judge Canada in economic terms alone or simply think of it in economic terms. We have to balance the economic and the political, and the political means that there must be government intervention in the right measure to ensure that our economy works vis-a-vis the American economy and the economies of the other trading blocs in the world such as the European community, Japan and so on. Our survival in this country, our survival politically, economically, socially and culturally, depends upon the right amount of intervention by Canadian Governments.
The greatest years of prosperity in Canada were those years when the Government played an active role with the private sector. It was hot those years when the Government was absent or when the Government withdrew. The years we had the least unemployment and the greatest growth was when there was a proper partnership between Government and the private sector.
In arguing for a certain amount of stimulation, I am not arguing for over-regulation, undue centralization or waste. Not at all. We can have stimulus; intervention into the economy without undue regulation, without undue centralization and waste. These are not necessary. These were not necessary in the past when we had great years of economic boom in Canada.
I have been critical of the Government's policy. The Government seems to say, if we believe the speeches of the Minister of Finance and other economic Ministers in the Government, that to a great extent the deficit is responsible for unemployment and, therefore, to attack the deficit the Government should withdraw from programs and thereby stimulate the economy. If it withdraws, the Government argues, the private sector will pick up things and produce the jobs which are required. 1 do not support that policy. I do not think it will work.
They may say in response that our policies did not work either, and they have said that. I do not agree. Our policies were not perfect, but I would argue that they worked better and eventually would have brought more success to solving these problems than their policy. We believe in stimulating the economy and we believe in goals.
Let us look at the programs which were set up under previous Liberal Governments. There was the establishment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which was transformed into DRIE. There were the policies of the Department of Supply and Services to ensure that through the purchasing policy of the Government we stimulated employment in different parts of the country. There were transportation policies to double track the railways, and there were housing policies. All these things were in conjunction with the creation of jobs and the stimulation of the economy. I could continue to list the type of programs we put into effect- LEAD, the job corp, career access, Canada Works and so on. Liberal Governments have always made a very substantial commitment to job stimulation.
As an example I should like to refer to a report which talked about the period from 1980 to 1985. It indicated that the
April 16, 1985

Government's vigorous response to the need for direct employment action was reflected in the total spending figures for the five fiscal years ending March 31, 1985. For direct job creation in that period, $3.8 billion was spent, rising from $310 million per year in 1980-81 to $1.2 billion in 1984-85. That shows a Liberal commitment to direct job creation. With respect to human resources training, that is training and retraining programs, $5 billion was spent during that period, rising from $800 million to $1.2 billion per year over the same period of time. The total for direct job creation and human resources training under Liberal Governments over the past five years comes to $8.5 billion.
They say that our programs did not work. I admit that all things are relative, but in the years when Mr. Trudeau was Prime Minister from 1968 until he resigned last year, three million jobs were created. There were 40 per cent more Canadians employed in 1984 than there were in 1968. That compares with the other six leading countries of this world which only had an increase of 13 per cent. During that period in Canada, our labour force grew at twice the rate of the six largest OECD countries. Even in the year coming out of the recession, in 1983, there were 400,000 new jobs created, although the labour force in that year grew 58 per cent faster than in the United States.
My point is that through stimulative programs, the problem was being attacked. It was being attacked despite very complex and difficult problems, despite a very fast growing labour force. We could all be more tolerant of the Conservatives and more sympathetic to their position today if they had been honest during the election campaign, if they had been frank during the election campaign and admitted at that time, as they are doing now, that the problems are complex and difficult, that in a free economy, in a free society there are no quick fixes. During the election campaign they had all the answers. I refer again, because I think the Canadian people must be reminded of this, to the statement of the Prime Minister on July 5 in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, when he said:
You are going to see tens upon tens of thousands of jobs being created just as quickly as a new Government can be sworn in.
We know how ridiculous that statement was. It was not honest. It was not a frank assessment of the economic situation in Canada. The Canadian people have to be reminded of that. As I said a few minutes ago, we would be more tolerant today of the problems and approaches of the Government if it had been frank during the election campaign.
There are some who believe that if you do stimulate the economy to create the jobs, you will bring back inflation and that inflation will get out of hand. I want to indicate that that is not necessary. Several countries have dealt with both problems. It is not a question of dealing either with inflation or unemployment. You can deal with both at the same time. I will refer to some other countries with which we trade.
Supply
In Japan in 1983, the unemployment rate was 2.7 per cent and the inflation rate was 1.8 per cent. There was quite considerable success on both counts. In Austria, the unemployment rate was 4.5 per cent and the inflation rate 3.8 per cent, in Norway there was 3.3 per cent unemployment and a 7.1 per cent inflation, and in Sweden there was 3.5 per cent unemployment and a 9.2 per cent inflation.
The point is that you can do both. I believe this should be done through setting goals, establishing stimulative programs, making our Canadian industry as efficient and competitive as possible to compete with those countries, by having the proper programs for retraining and mobility and by making adjustments in our work time schedule. That means shorter work weeks, longer holidays, incentives for early retirement and so on.
There are a lot of jobs out there. Last year before the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, the Canadian Council on Social Development indicated to us that it alone had discovered 300,000 jobs in its area of concern which had to be created but were not being created because there was not enough financing to put those jobs on line.
The Government has not done very much. It put into place the Canada Works Program for this winter. That was a Liberal program. We congratulate it. It was the right thing to do. The Government put Challenge '85 in place for next summer. That is a poor copy of the Summer Works Program of last year. Aside from that, it has done nothing. The statement in Regina in February at the First Ministers' Conference was a lot of promises and a lot of proposals, but they have not been put into effect. They have not been implemented. There is no action yet, only discussion and study.
I was very disappointed with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). I wanted to ask her a question on this, Mr. Speaker, but you did not recognize me. She praised the members of the New Democratic Party for their task force. I agree that it was a very good idea. At the same time, in attempting to be very partisan, she said that the Conservatives believe in consultation, the NDP believe in consultation, but the Liberals obviously do not. I want to put on record again the consultation that took place in the last Parliament with respect to unemployment.
The task force, of which I was Chairman and of which the Hon. Member from Calgary was Vice-Chairman, entitled Employment Opportunities for the '80s, heard over 342 groups and witnesses all across this country. It was a very strong consultative process. Then there was the task force on skilled development, the program Paid Educational Leave, the task force on major capital projects, the task force "In the Chips" regarding technology and employment, the task force on labour market development, the House of Commons committee on profit sharing. I could go on and on.
I will conclude by saying that we need goals and stimulus. What we need in this country is a six and five program for unemployment and to put behind it the same political will as

Second, regarding the new approach taken in Regina and what the critics have to say about it, I think that what happened in Regina is that for the first time the Federal Government and the provinces were able to agree on six new ways to create jobs.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to Challenge '85, the Minister announced certain figures in which she claims great success for the program. She says it has already created so many jobs. I want to wait and see if those jobs are in fact created because I do not see that happening in my riding. In my riding, there seems to be more or less what we had last year. We will wait and see.
Just before Easter, a question was put to the Minister of Employment and Immigration by a Conservative Member regarding how many applications were granted in the private sector under Challenge '85. The Minister rose and said that the answer was 29,000. We immediately phoned her office and asked how many jobs were created under Challenge '85 through municipalities and community organizations. A representative in the Minister's office told us that that was not public information and that we could not receive that information. I know that a lot of the groups that were being helped last year like associations for the blind and daycare centres are being left out this year. They are not receiving the same funding. They are getting a smaller slice of the pie this year than they did last year.
Companies that make toilet seats or ice cream cones are getting a bigger share of the pie than groups that are helping the impoverished, the lame, the crippled and the aged. While I am not against that, I am opposed to the fact that there is not a greater share of the program for the community groups. We will wait until the program is over to judge whether or not it has been a success. We will be back here next fall and we will see then the results of the program.

Mr. Speaker, everyone begins by saying that it is a pleasure to take part in a debate such as this one. In fact, it is not. The truth of the master is that I would much rather that there was no necessity for a debate such as this, that the Government had brought forward proposals that had begun to address the problems of those who are unemployed and that it had started to talk about the needs of those who have been neglected for 10, 20 or 30 years.
Let me first focus upon the issue about which we are speaking. We are talking about a motion that calls upon the Government to bring in immediately stimulative proposals to reduce unemployment by a minimum of 2.5 per cent within the next 12 months. We based our need for putting this motion forward on the fact that the Government has failed to live up to its commitment to make job creation its number one priority. Instead of living up to that commitment, the Government has pursued cut-backs which have in fact led to unemployment in three out of the last four months. That is what we are debating here today. We are debating whether or not the Government has in fact lived up to the commitments that it made prior to the 1984 election.
I believe any fair-minded individual looking at the record of the Government could not help but come to the conclusion that the Government has failed miserably to live up to its commitment. In fact, one could not help but come to the conclusion that at the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that if the Tories were elected, they would immediately create tens of thousands of new jobs, that commitment was made without the benefit of the support of the Prime Minister's colleagues, without the understanding of the problems of Canada and in fact was made simply for the purpose of achieving for the Conservative Party additional votes at the polls on a promise it never intended to keep and which has been cast aside.
In her comments, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) said that we have to have confidence in Canada's future. I do not disagree with that. I think we have to have confidence. There is no other land with such an abundance of resources as Canada. There is no other land in the world that has available to it the kind of access that we have to the markets of the world, should we choose to use it. Over many, many years, however, the difficulty has been that Canada's economic infrastructure has not been permitted to pursue the markets of the world in an attempt to enhance the manufacturing capacity of this country. It has not been permitted to manufacture products for world distribution. It was denied that opportunity by virtue of the fact that, to a large extent, Canada's employers are branch plants of American and European employers who have no interest in allowing the Canadian economy to grow and compete with the parent

companies' home bases. That has been one of the fundamental problems that has confronted Canada and therefore confronted the need to develop an over-all economic strategy that would involve the major component parts of the economy including the major manufacturers. That has been one of the inhibiting factors to Canada's realization of a long-term goal that we could and should be a major part of the economic thrust of the world. We cannot begin to deal with Canada's fundamental problems until we begin to deal with the basic structure of the manufacturing sector. We must create policy which will encourage those in the manufacturing sector to realize both the domestic requirements and the international potentials. They must be freed from the shackles which have been imposed upon them by Governments and the administrative head offices of their enterprises.
The Minister asked us to deal with facts. I would like to deal with some of the facts as I see them.
The first fact is that there are 1.3 million people unemployed today. There is nothing being done by the Government to move in an attempt to create for those people-many of whom are long-term unemployed-the opportunity to get back to work.
The second fact is that unemployment has risen in three of the last four months. It is a fact that job creation, both private and public, has been inadequate in Canada for the last five years. It is a fact that this Government, by virtue of its economic statement in November, moved to eliminate jobs in Canada.
It is a fact that the youth unemployment program which was brought forward by the Government had, as a major component, the involvement of the private sector. However, companies in the private sector in many cases were in the position in which they had already laid off people and were unable, even if they had been willing, to participate and to create the employment which we require.
It is a fact that unemployment among those who are disabled in Canada is now running upward of 60 per cent of those who would be eligible to become employed. In looking at those numbers we must bear in mind that 10 per cent of our population falls into the category of being disabled.
It is a fact that private initiative in Canada has been lagging since the middle 1970s. It is a fact that this Government moved to remove $1 billion from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada in September, 1984. The effect of that move was devastating on consumers, consumer-oriented manufacturers, and those who provide the services in almost every community in Canada.
It is a fact that not one program was brought forward by the Government which was specifically aimed at meeting the problems of those people who fall into the category of being between the ages of 55 and 65. Those people have given years and years of hard work in an attempt to hold their families together and build society, but not one program has been aimed at assisting them. Now they find that the plant or
factory in which they worked, the mine, the office or the store by which they were employed no longer requires their services. There is not a single community in Canada which does not provide an adequate example of people who have spent a lifetime working in the community, building and developing the resources in that community, who now discover, as a result of the economic downturn, that they have been cast out as if they were trash. Not one program from this Government has been aimed specifically at trying to combat that problem.
It is a fact that there is not a special municipal project oriented as an employment-type program worth its name. We could visit any community and ask the local mayor, council and local community groups if there are not projects which are both necessary and could be proceeded with quickly if the funding were available. Every community which I have visited,-whether it be in the Yukon where I was last weekend, southern Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia or the Maritime Provinces-without exception, has projects which are both necessary and could be proceeded with quickly if the funding were made available. But this Government has failed to come forward with the necessary funding. It is clear that money spent on projects in local communities would enhance the value of Canada.
If a new sewage, sanitation or disposal plant were built in a community, it would enhance the value of the community and, therefore, the value of the country as a whole. There could be a major road rebuilding program which would enhance the value of a community and, therefore, the country as a whole. The money which would be spent on those kinds of projects would remain in Canada. The employment which would be created from those kinds of expenditures would be employment at the local level for people who are now unemployed and who ought to be working. The materials which would be used in undertaking those kinds of projects would come from Canada, would be manufactured by Canadians, and would be put in place by Canadians. Therefore, we in this country would derive 100 per cent of the benefit. It is a fact that this Government refused to move forward on that front in order to try to meet the needs of the communities.
It is a fact that there has been no emphasis placed by this Government on the problems of single-industry towns. We could go to the Eastern Townships of Quebec and, without exception, we would see that town after town is a single-industry based town. Those single industries are now under tremendous pressure in many cases. Of course, the most recent case occurred in Windsor, and it took the Prime Minister himself to intervene, to go in with money after the opposition Parties had pressured the Government to do that. It could have been done a month or two months previously, but it had to be held off so the Prime Minister could get the maximum benefit from the announcement. Those people sat in despair. They were concerned about their futures. They recognized that everything for which they had worked was in jeopardy. But this Government waited until the Prime Minister had his hair cut and put on a new suit before the statement was made. The statement ought to have been made months before.

It is a fact that there has been absolutely no resource sector priorization. The forest industry, which is the backbone of so many communities across Canada, is an example. Where is the money for the continuing requirements of the forest industry? When has the Government said that it would move on that front in order to put the tens of thousands of people, who have been unemployed for the better part of the last two years, back to work? The Government has failed to come forward with a single program to combat that particular problem, regardless of whether it exists in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec or the Maritimes.
It is a fact that this Government seems to be determined to foist on to the backs of the working people the tremendous pressures which flow from the economic mismanagement of years of Liberal administration at the federal level and years of Conservative administration at the provincial level. This Government is unable or unwilling to meet the demands of establishing a clear economic path for Canada which would satisfy our needs in the long run, while, at the same time, providing the necessary support for the people who are being asked to carry the enormous burdens of unemployment during this, hopefully, short-run period of economic uncertainty. And the facts go on.
It is a fact, for example, that $1.5 billion could be found for the multi-national oil companies by this Government but it could not find the necessary hundreds of thousands of dollars in order to meet the demands and requirements of other equally important parts of Canada's economy. It is a fact that when the Canadian Commercial Bank went under, the Government could find $60 million from a Budget in which it claimed there was no money available. The Government could find $60 million to bail out the Canadian Commercial Bank, but when the farmers of this country were going bankrupt in record numbers, it could not even find it in its heart to commiserate, never mind finding the money to assist in offsetting the losses which were being incurred. It is a fact that when the small business people of this country were looking to the Government for some assistance when high interest rates were the order of the day-just some months ago-this Government could not find any way to help because, after all, the coffers of the Government were extended to the absolute maximum; there was no more money. But when the multi-nationals needed $1.5 billion, when the Commercial Bank needed $60 million, the Government just reached back, as if it was nothing, took the money out of the bag and said, "There it is, guys. Go to it. You are our friends. The others are not. We'll look after you. The hell with everyone else". That is the Government we are addressing today.

ment to do what is right rather than what is expedient. In my own community I find that plants are closing. The previous Government funded the take-over of Admiral by Inglis. We asked the previous Government to make some provision for guaranteeing the jobs of those who were already working for Inglis, to take some steps to protect those people from the potential job losses which were evident in the future. The previous Liberal administration did not take the necessary steps. Now I ask the Minister who is in charge of regional economic expansion if he will take some steps, but he tells me he cannot, it is a rationalization process and if those people lose their jobs, that's just too bad. He said it in a nicer way, perhaps, that he does not feel it would be appropriate to intervene in any way.
Why is it not appropriate to intervene in a situation where a company is closing down in one place, opening up in another, and throwing families out onto the street? Why is that not appropriate action for a Government? Why is it not appropriate for the Government to sit down with companies which are closing down simply in order to maximize profits which are already significantly higher than need be? Why is it not appropriate for a Government to sit down and talk to them about their obligation to the community in which they are located? I suggest that that is part of the problem with this Government. It is oriented to bigness, anything that's big, anything to do with millions of dollars and billions of dollars, but when it comes right down to ordinary people who are unemployed and who need some help and someone to stand up for them, where is this Government? It is nowhere to be found. And that is what is wrong with this Government.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, we presented a whole host of very reasonable suggestions as to how this question could be dealt with. Not only did we ask the Government to spend money wisely and well but we even suggested how the Government might raise the necessary money. We suggested the adjustments which could be made in the expenditure patterns in order to ensure that the money we were saying could be spent, was spent without an inordinate increase in the deficit. But what does the Government do? It stands up and tells us, "We still cannot afford to go ahead with it. It is unfortunate. We feel sorry for the people who are detrimentally affected, but we just can't see a way to raise that money".
Why can Government not raise the money we are suggesting should be raised? Its corporate friends are now being asked to donate a hundred dollars to the Brian Mulroney fund in Quebec so that they can have direct access to the Government. That is why. It is because this Government operates on patronage and patronage alone. It is because this Government does not give a damn about the ordinary individual no matter what it says. Mr. Speaker, my question has two parts. I heard my hon. friend say earlier that we were spending money and were prepared to give money to multinational corporations without really doing an in-depth study. What is the Government supposed to do when a company which made a profit of $90 or $95 million last year and distributed over $200 million in dividends in the past eight years, turns around and asks the Government for $100 million? The same company did not invest any capital during the last 30 years because it wanted to close the plant, but all of a sudden it found that there were new possibilities on the market. What did the Government do? It looked at the matter from a different perspective and made the company face up to its own responsibilities.
My hon. friend also said that there were no programs for municipalities that are in fact company towns, or programs for the 45 and up age group. He knows perfectly well that in Regina, the federal and provincial governments agreed to set up two of those programs, as part of the six avenues for job creation now being developed as a result of the Regina Conference. We are now working on these programs to have everything ready by next September. Even the report published after the NDP group held its consultations across Canada made it quite clear that the first requirement for setting up a job creation program was to have federal, provincial and municipal authorities working together. That is what we started off doing, and we are going to bring the resulting programs to the country. That is what we are working on, including these two specific programs.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary could tell us what new information became available in Windsor that was not available a month ago. And how would he relate the attitude in Windsor to the attitude taken by the Government to the multi-national oil companies which will take from the federal Treasury of Canada $1.5 billion that they do not need either? They will receive money which can be spent by them to undertake projects that they were already being compensated for through the tax structure. I do not understand how the Government can have this double standard.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question and I will follow it with a comment. I appreciated the speech of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans). As many of the Hon. Members in this room would expect, I was interested when he referred-

Member he did talk about the need to provide funding for Canadian municipalities. because I think it is a step in the right direction considering the policies of this Government, but does it mean that the NDP also has abandoned a full employment policy?

Mr. Speaker, jobs, jobs, jobs. We in the Conservative Party of Canada ran an election campaign on jobs and said we would create jobs. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has reminded the House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that as soon as we changed Governments there would be tens of thousands of new jobs. Well, I stand here in this House today with statistics from the first six months of this Government's life which indicate there are 112,000 Canadians working today who would not have had a job under the other Government. When you talk about tens of thousands of jobs, 10,000 into
112,000	goes 11 times; that is 11 times we have kept that promise in the first six months. But we are not satisfied and we will do better and I hope they begin to recognize what we have been doing for this country.
Not only have we created those 112,000 new jobs, which means new taxpayers instead of tax spenders, but let us compare that with the same period of time in 1983 and 1984, September to March. At that time, under the previous Government unemployment in this country went up by 38,000 people. The record of this Government in a comparable period of time in 1984-85 is that of 48,000 fewer unemployed. The total change of 38,000 plus 48,000 is 86,000 jobs, and that is an important statistic.
Let me give you a third statistic which is also important. Ever since this country had the opportunity to throw out the previous Government there has been a change in the participation rate. It has gone up because people have hope. They believed the Prime Minister of this country and the Conservative Members during the election that we would dedicate our efforts to straightening out the economy and create jobs for Canadians.
