Mr. Speaker, tomorrow, April 17, marks a historic date for Canada's disabled people. As of Wednesday, discrimination based on physical and mental disability will be unconstitutional.
Disabled people in Canada have fought long and hard for a fair chance to do many things most of us take for granted. For example, the simple process of gathering information from newspapers, books, and magazines can be difficult, if not impossible, for a blind person.
Last week 1 had the opportunity of touring, with the Chairman of the Board of the Metropolitan Toronto Library Board, Mr. Irv Sherman, the newly opened Metro Toronto Library Centre for disabled persons. This excellent centre has a variety of information services for disabled people, including a Kurz-weil Reading Machine that actually reads aloud from a printed text in a synthetic voice.
On the eve of the implementation of equality rights, I urge the Government to continue to open the door of opportunity for Canada's disabled people.

subtopic: DELAY IN COMPLETING AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA
DELAY IN COMPLETING AGREEMENT WITH BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is still no federal-provincial forestry agreement in place in British Columbia in spite of Conservative promises of federal-provincial co-operation and help to the forest industry. While waiting for that agreement to be signed, 2,300 workers in the Canada Works Forestry Program face lay-offs. Last week I met over 100 of these men and women on their last day of work. Funding had run out, and new funds had not been allocated.
These people want to know why negotiations always have to wait until the last minute. As one worker said, maybe if more of the people doing the negotiating lived hand-to-mouth like the workers who depend on the programs, they would not be quite so casual in the way in which they negotiate for new funds.
It now appears that the Department of Employment and Immigration has offered to pay wages, but not overhead, for the program until the end of June. The companies object to paying anything at all, even though their forest lands get the benefit of the work that is being done. We can only ask if this is an example of the much touted "new mood of co-operation" between the Conservative Government and private business. Is this the kind of free enterprise that is going to create jobs for two million out-of-work Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, the sign reads "Government For Sale". For $100 you can now join the Brian Mulroney Club. Membership will allow you access to your Member of Parliament, as unbelievable as that may seem, but it is not guaranteed that you will find a solution to your problem. Tory organizers expect many members to join within months.
The Government was elected to serve Canadians, not to sell their services. This is the most outrageous of all the atrocities that have been perpetrated by the Conservative Party on the people of Canada. What can we expect next? Tory Members peddling Brian Mulroney's picture for $10 to their supporters in their own constituencies?
To all Tory Members in the House I say that we on this side of the House we do not charge to help the people of Canada. Mr. Speaker, please advise the constituents of other ridings that the Liberals are here to serve everyone, rich and poor alike.

Mr. Speaker, the issue of unlicensed utility wheat has received considerable press in the past, not only in recent weeks but over the past years. One has only to look at the various strains that have been developed in an attempt to maximize production to be aware of this.
We have seen the introduction of triticale, and the development and licensing of HY320 as examples of this. It was only natural that farmers, who are neighbours in spite of the fact that the Canada-U.S. border separates their farms, would discuss and exchange not only ideas but seed as well. To ignore
April 16, 1985

this fact, and many other problems of agriculture, was a tactic often employed by the previous Liberal administration.
Calling together all interested parties, from growers to grain company officials, particularly those who represent companies co-operatively owned by the producers, demonstrates that the consultative process is alive and well in the Government. We recognize that agriculture is a pillar of the Canadian economy and are trying to provide another option for hard-pressed producers. I commend the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board for his actions, and call on all Members of the House to applaud him for his insight in dealing with this problem.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow marks the fiftieth anniversary of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, an organization which has become part of the very fabric of the Prairies. Established by a Conservative Government on April 17, 1935, the PFRA was born at a time of unprecedented drought conditions in the rural west. Through its emphasis on long-term planning and conservation, the PFRA helped western agriculture to survive and, later, to prosper. For example, the Palliser triangle, once the infamous dust bowl of the Prairies, is again agriculturally productive, thanks in large part to the PFRA.
Tonight at the University of Manitoba this historic anniversary is being marked with a seminar attended by numerous experts in water and soil conservation who will discuss the organization's past and its future. All this comes at a time when consideration is being given to basic structural changes in the PFRA.
1 commend my colleague, the Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), for putting forth recommendations which will be considered by the Agriculture Committee in the near future. Apart from these recommendations, Mr. Speaker, agricultural technology and growing public awareness about conservation have created new challenges for this organization.
I am confident that, just as it met its goals in the past, the PFRA will rise to the challenges of the future. I congratulate PFRA officials on this historic occasion. I wish them every success in their deliberations this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to send a warning to all Canadians who are concerned about a growing trend by Governments seriously to misrepresent facts for their own partisan purposes.
In his classic novel 1984 George Orwell presented a chilling portrait of a Government that used the control of language as a means to control its people. It consciously and insidiously twisted and distorted the meaning of words until the resulting language, called newspeak, proclaimed that love was hate, war was peace, and freedom was slavery.
Since the Government was elected a short seven months ago, the proliferation of newspeak has grown to alarming proportions. Nowhere is this more apparent than when it comes to the Government's pronouncements on unemployment. Yesterday's performance by that master of newspeak himself, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), indicates that the level of misrepresentation by the Government has reached new heights.
Yesterday the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) pointed out that the rate of job creation in the last six months is lower than in the previous six months, and that in fact unemployment has increased in three of the last four months. Yet the Prime Minister continues to say that there has been "a rebirth in confidence in the private sector resulting in job creation". There are 65,000 more Canadians unemployed today than when the Prime Minister assumed office. These are the facts, yet the Government will have us believe otherwise.
It is a dangerous practice to deny the truth. One could foresee the day when the Government creates a Minister of Information to tell what is truth and what is not. Canadians do not want their Government to tell them that black is white, or that unemployment is going down when in fact it is going up.
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time is expired.

Mr. Speaker, a Tory is a Tory is a very sad story for the City of Hamilton. Just as our tight-lipped Premier was in Hamilton announcing the creation of a measely 10 jobs, the federal Government was refusing to honour its commitment of $2.4 million for the upgrading of the regional incinerator. It would be funny if it were not such a threat to the health of the people of Hamilton. This upgrading is absolutely critical because SWARU has been emitting dioxins into the air breathed by hundreds of thousands of people in the Niagara region. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) can find $1 billion for oil companies, but she cannot find $2.4 million to protect Hamiltonians from cancer causing agents.
This political story does not end here. The regional chairman, who also happens to be a current candidate for the Tories in Ontario, sent a telex to the Ministers involved to say that this funding was critical and the freeze was a severe shock. The candidate sent copies to the Members for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson) and Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), but skipped right

April 16, 1985
over the riding of Hamilton East where the residents will be most affected by the cut-back.
The Tory candidate thought it was more important to protect the Government than to protect the citizens of Hamilton. She has hidden the truth from the Opposition and shown that her only interest is in protecting fellow Conservatives. The Tories in Ontario have always left Hamilton in the cold, except when it came to foisting schemes of regional government and rapid transit on the people. Now we see that their Ottawa cousins are cut from the same sackcloth.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after having the privilege of accompanying the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on his recent visit to the Soviet Union, I must say that the Minister did a remarkable job in situations and circumstances that were not always easy.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this trip was, first and foremost, to provide for a better mutual understanding between our two countries, to establish a relationship with the Soviets and to re-establish lines of communications which had been neglected for more than a year.
Mr. Speaker, during our visits to Leningrad, Novosibirsk, Moscow and Kiev, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was always clear and consistent in what he had to say. Although our two countries will always have political differences, we must seek, above all, the points of interest we have in common and maintain a constant dialogue. Oh, oh!

Kenora to Thunder Bay. Since the Minister of Transport is responsible for the transportation of dangerous goods, I should like to ask him whether further measures are contemplated under that Act. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is correct. There has been consultation and there has been action. That is as soon as it is practically possible to put these regulations in place. It has been done in consultation with the industry, and there has been a certain degree of hardship imposed. Nonetheless, that announcement has been made. Naturally, when the regulations become effective, all transportation of dangerous goods in Canada and, indeed, trans-border, will have to conform to those regulations.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. My constituents will not be pleased to know that they have to wait until the tourist season for protection. Will he assure the House that the situation will be reviewed in light of this experience?

Mr. Speaker, I assure the Hon. Member, and all Hon. Members of the House, that we are taking this issue seriously. We are showing leadership. The fact of the matter is that we accelerated the proclamation of the regulations under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act by several months. That took some convincing, and it took a lot of consultation. As I said earlier, my departmental officials are working very closely with the Department of the Environment for the Province of Ontario to ensure that an adequate investigation is carried out, and to ensure that all necessary precautions were in fact followed and will be followed in the future.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Langdon:
That this House calls upon the Government to immediately bring in stimulative proposals to reduce unemployment by a minimum of 2.5 per cent within the next 12 months, given the failure of the Government to live up to its commitment to make job-creation its number one priority, and its pursuit, instead, of a policy of cut-backs which has led to a rise in unemployment in three of the last four months.

Mr. Speaker, I promised Hon. Members of the House this morning that I would continue to expand on my opening remarks. In listening to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), who was the second speaker for the New Democratic Party this morning, I wondered if he could recognize a government program or policy which created a job because he stood and talked about the Western Accord which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) signed some two and a half weeks ago. I would just like to read some of the headlines in the newspapers in my riding which flow directly from that Accord. The Calgary Herald states, "Demand for Engineers on the Upswing. Cranes May Once Again Break Skyline". Another headline reads, "Large Scale Energy Projects Seen Possible". The last, and perhaps the most important headline, Mr. Speaker, reads, "Student Job Picture Brighter". That Mr. Speaker, is a piece of public policy which creates jobs.
I sat in this House and watched the Liberal Government with its majority ram down the throats of Canadians, without sufficient thought, a piece of public policy in the energy field which chased $18 billion of capital out of this country. That is 18 thousand million dollars which was chased out of Canada into the United States of America, Australia, the Arab States, Mexico, or somewhere else, along with the jobs. We, in essence, through a single piece of public policy, were in the business of exporting jobs. And when the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain stands in this Chamber, having been a part of all that experience, and fails to recognize that the complete abandonment of the National Energy Program is the greatest single piece of job-generating public policy that any Government has brought forward in this country in recent memory, then I simply feel sorry for his capacity to learn from experience.
The New Democratic Party convened a task force which went around the country hearing witnesses. The task force wrote a report and today we have an Opposition Day based on an NDP motion. In the report of the task force there is some good news and some bad news. If I could just start, in the interests of non-partisan debate, with the good news, I would suggest that in the 72 recommendations there are an awful lot which are copied from previous Progressive Conservative Party task force reports and the report of the parliamentary subcommittee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s. That is the
April 16, 1985

good news. The even better news is that the new Government, in a brief period of six months, has acted on many of those recommendations and by the time the NDP laid the report on the table, those particular policies were under way and in many cases implemented. I draw attention particularly to the NDP recommendation that the Government of Canada make every effort to purchase from Canadian suppliers. That is being done. That was one of the first things the new Government set in train.
There is a recommendation that foreign firms with subsidiary branch plants in Canada be required, be asked, be encouraged, whatever, to put more investment into this country, to produce more goods within this country. And, Mr. Speaker, every step this Government has taken-not in one single way but in lots of ways-has been dedicated in part toward that end. The whole issue of Investment Canada which the Opposition has tried to filibuster is simply going in the direction of the recommendation. Underlying everything is the need for business confidence if we are going to get the economy turned around and get those jobs back. Certainly by its behaviours this Government has shown that it is going in that direction. That is the good news, Mr. Speaker, the extent to which the report copies from previous reports and already implemented strategy.
It almost makes me sad to have to stand in this Chamber, having read the report, knowing there were university academics involved in its preparation, because it will perhaps mislead some people. But I am even more disturbed by what appears to me to be some fatal flaws in logic. One of the key thoughts behind the report is that the federal deficit should be expanded for the purpose of creating jobs. They lay out some data and tell us that since 1975, when the Government moved to restraint, unemployment went from 6.9 per cent to 11 per cent. Therefore, they say, restraint is bad and a bigger deficit is good. But, Mr. Speaker, the federal deficit went up in that decade and is now 10 times larger than it was in 1975. How on earth could a university-trained person make the statement that the deficit increasing 10 times in 10 years is restraint? It defies logic. There has been no restraint in Canada. There has been no common sense in Canada. To conclude on the basis of the Canadian experience that restraint does not work is pure lunacy and would get you flunked in any basic economics course in the country.
When I was elected to this House some 17 cents out of every tax dollar went to pay interest on the public debt. That was six years ago. Today it is close to 36 cents. We used to have 83 cents out of every tax dollar to spend on programs, and now we have 64 cents. That is what the increase in the deficit has done. It means that the federal Government has to borrow 92 per cent of the projected savings of Canadians. That leaves 8 per cent for Canadians to buy a car, a home or a boat. That is why we have had to reach out to borrow money abroad, and when you do that you have to send interest payments out of the country. So following this whole period of economic insani-
Supply
ty and excessive borrowing we have increasing unemployment. That is the reality.
The NDP talks about Canadians wanting government leadership in four main areas. It has met groups of people, talked to Canadians, listened to them, and it says we need leadership in four key areas. Job expansion is the top priority, and we agree. We agreed during the election and we agree today. We have to get a million and a half people back to work. Another of those four key areas was removing inequities in employment. We believe that is true and we commend the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) for moving so swiftly on the Abella report to do something concrete and positive which has been needed for a long time. We agree that Canadians see that as a key area and we are pleased to have made a start. The third area is that of tax reform, and here also we believe the NDP is right; Canadians want tax reform. We may disagree on the kind of reform or on some of the details, but Canadians want it, and let me tell the NDP that the Western Accord is a revision of Canadian tax policy with enormous job creation potential. We believe it is something the voters of this country wanted and are glad they got. We will see other examples of tax policy changes.
We now come to the fourth area, that of more direct government involvement in productive investment. But Canadians did not tell the NDP that that is what they wanted. If the NDP gerrymandered specific groups, they may have got that message, but that is the only way. Either that or the NDP invented this as the fourth key area to go along with the ideology with which it started. But that is not something that Canadians believe. Canadians have had very little experience with direct government investment that has been productive. By and large, their experience is that the least productive way to go about things is through direct government involvement. It leads in many, many cases to waste and inefficiency and there are temptations for patronage and all kinds of negative things. We believe-and I think any well conducted scientific poll would support the notion-that Canadians want Government out of the direct investment field. They want private sector investment. They want real long-term jobs. They want jobs with career potential, jobs which exist because there is a product or service that somebody wants to purchase. That is where efficiency comes from. That is where the long-term economic health of this nation comes from. That is is where progress comes from.
There is a committee of this House of Commons, the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, where we have laboured long and hard since the middle of January on our investigation of immigration. We have heard a lot of witnesses and produced the first and second reports. We are now writing the third report and beginning investigation today into another area, that of refugees. The second report said that, where immigration was concerned, we should have a population goal in mind. We believe that that goal should be an increase in the population and that immigration is an important factor in increasing Canada's population. Because of birth and death rates we will require increased immigration.

April 16, 1985
Supply
But we said that, in dealing with that increase, we should take a portion-right now about 2 per cent, perhaps in time that number will be 3 per cent or even 4 per cent-and go around the world to seek out entrepreneurs, people with cash, people with experience, people with a product who want to come to Canada with their families and create businesses and jobs for Canadians. This is a job-creation program through immigration. It would not disturb family reunification or refugees; in fact, there would be more of those. We said, let us take a part of that increase and create jobs for Canadians. We have a little bit of experience which suggests that the few people in that category we have let in have created 24,000 jobs already. They brought an average of $800,000 of equity capital apiece and created 24,000 jobs. If we can expand that and make it 10 times larger, that would be a quarter of a million jobs at a time when we have 1.5 million unemployed people.
The NDP and the Liberals went to a press conference and said that they do not want that job creation. That is the essence of what they said. They said they would rather play politics on the heads of Canadians than do something sane and sensible in terms of job creation in the country such as encouraging the people with business ideas and capital expenditures to create jobs and futures for Canadians. The NDP and the Liberals said publicly that that is a bad idea. If they want to say publicly that that is a bad idea, I simply suggest to them that they are beginning, if they have not already done so, to lose any credibility they may have had on the job-creation issue. That job-creation idea does not cost the taxpayers a dime. It could produce jobs for one-quarter of a million people. When they reverse their stand on that it may be worth-while to look at some of their other ideas.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of his speech before the break the Hon. Member referred to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) promise during the election campaign that they would create tens upon tens of thousands of jobs. The Hon. Member said that they had achieved that promise and created 100,000 jobs. Of course he did not say that they have also cancelled and lost hundreds of thousands of jobs. How else can it be explained that in August of 1984 the unemployment rate was 11.2 per cent and in March, nearly seven months after they took office, the rate is still 11.2 per cent? Of course some new jobs were created, but at the same time they cut a lot of jobs in the Public Service, the cultural agencies, the CBC, and the Department of the Environment. Surely when the Prime Minister made those promises during the election campaign he meant that there would be additional jobs created rather than a total loss in jobs. I think the Hon. Member should be honest and fair in talking about this. I would like him to explain this. Did the Prime Minister mean that while jobs would be created they would also cut out jobs? Why did he not say that during the election campaign? Why was he not frank with the Canadian people?
With regard to the immigration report that the committee produced a week or so ago, I must remind the Hon. Member
that the entrepreneurial program was started by a Liberal Government. It was started by the Member right here when he was Minister. We are not opposed to the entrepreneurial program. We started it. We are opposed to the way in which the recommendation was made which gave priority to people in a certain category, people with money. We are opposed to that and to other parts of the report, but we are not opposed to the entrepreneurial program. That was our program.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member reads the report. He voted against it. It does not say anything about priority for people with money, not one single word. I challenge him to come to the House with the report and show me where it says that.
With regard to the other issue which the Hon. Member raised, there are adjusted and unadjusted figures which come out of the labour force survey. The only honest, decent comparison is year over year. We have just been through March of 1985. There were 10,864,000 Canadians employed in March of 1985 and 10,595,000 Canadians employed in March of 1984. This March there were 269,000 more people employed than last year in the same month. That is progress, Mr. Speaker. The month before it was 217,000. That is the record of the Government. Whatever crib sheet the Member is cribbing from was created somewhere in Alice in Wonderland. It does not relate to the true job situation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address the portions of the intervention of the Hon. Member across the way which had anything to do with the debate today. I was interested to hear him say that he supported, in essence, the New Democratic Party call in the document for tax reform. I wonder whether he is serious. Are the tax changes which accorded benefits to the oil companies typical of what he foresees as tax reforms intended to benefit the people who spoke to us?
He tells us that no Canadians anywhere in the land want increased direct government expenditure of any kind. It may be appropriate for him to address the report of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities which quite clearly indicates that not only does it want direct government investment, but that it is necessary job-creating investment. Does the Hon. Member oppose the direct government investment involved in renewing our forests, fisheries, energy and education? Has he been across the country and seen that the needs which his own Government should support, in part through direct government investment, are the very needs the people of the country want to see met and which will create jobs?

Mr. Speaker, the issue of direct government involvement in productive investment is listed in the NDP report as one of the key areas. I do not quarrel with the reality that government funds will be better spent in the creation of a solid infrastructure. I do quarrel with the assertion in their document that Canadians would identify that as one of the four key areas. Starting with an ideological persuasion they used selective perception, drawing from two or three briefs, to arrive at that. It is not a conclusion that Canadians, chosen at
April 16, 1985

random, would reach. That is not the mood of the country. The mood is to do the things which create permanent, longterm jobs in the private sector. That is a justifiable mood because we have gone too far in the other direction.
They asked me whether I was in favour of tax breaks for the oil industry. Mr. Speaker, I have always been in favour of stopping and correcting the highway robbery of a single industry based in a single geographic region of the country, especially when that highway robbery chased jobs out of the country. Yes, I am in favour of a fair, just taxation policy that encourages jobs rather than discouraging them. That is the type of tax reform policy the country needs.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member just said that he knows what the mood of the country is. In relation to his elitist and narrow-minded immigration report, I ask how he got the mood of the country through that process when there were only seven witnesses from the Immigration Department. There was not a single witness from the immigrant aid societies, the ethnocultural groups, the unions, the economic community, or any Canadian who would be interested in the immigration policy of the country.
The Chairman and his band of right-wing Tories said in that report that no economic study was done, whether independently or by the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson), correlating the immigration targets and the employment and labour force goals of the Government. Despite that, they went on to say that they feel the country needs rich immigrants, which is also to overlook the fact that thousands upon thousands of immigrants of poor and average income came to the country and became successful businessmen. Thousands of those immigrants came to this country and took jobs that some Canadians did not want. Thousands of those immigrants came to this country and brought their skills and trades. All immigrants regardless of economic standing and status contribute to this economy by being consumers in this economy. They come here, they buy a home, they buy a car and so forth. While we as a Party support and encourage people with entrepreneurial spirit and capability to consider this country as their new homeland, we are suggesting that that is not the only way to prosperity and to build economic growth in Canada. Immigrants came here in the past. Immigrants can continue to come in the future and will add economically as well. Any immigration policy founded on the cornerstone of only rich immigrants is an insensitive, non-compassionate and regressive policy that is in keeping with this Government.

Mr. Speaker, over the last three years the Liberal Party of Canada choked off immigration and increased the proportion of rich people who came here under that policy. That is what the Hon. Member's Government did for the last three years.
Our Party is recommending an increase in immigration. Within that increase we want to create jobs. We believe we are on the right track. We have said not a single word about cutting off the kind of immigrants which the Hon. Member
Supply
talks about. All of us in this country come from stock of that kind. Our relatives came here with nothing. They created this country and they created our standard of living. We believe that must continue. The Hon. Member belongs to a party that was choking that concept to death. We are opening it up again, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).

Mr. Speaker, we have had several opportunities in this House over the last session to debate in various forms the issue of employment.
I want to compliment the Members of the New Democratic Party for having brought this motion forward and for once again giving Parliamentarians a chance to address what all of our constituents would say is one of the most important, if not the most important issue, along with that of the nuclear arms question, that we were sent here to look at and examine.
I want to say that we compliment the New Democrats as well on their initiative in going across the country to find out about job creation. Like many other Members of Parliament, we thought it was about time the Government found out about job creation. We are very glad that the New Democrats took the opportunity to do so and to share some of those findings with us.
What is important about the timing of this debate is that it comes at a time some five weeks before, we hope, the federal budget, that long awaited panacea promised us by various Members of the Government opposite that is to provide all the answers to problems raised. Every time a question has been asked in this House about where the jobs are, we hear them say, "Wait until the budget comes". Everything up to now has been preliminary. What is disturbing about that is we are still seeing fundamental conflicts taking place in the Conservative Government over the best way to approach the question of economic growth and job creation.
I do not dispute the Government's interest about this, we must express a very deep concern about the Government's ability and competence in this regard, and its ability to find the proper answers. What we have seen evidenced so far is a continual contradiction of goals and purposes, means and ends. The Conservative Government has replaced any coherence or consistency with public relations, flackery and promises for the future. We have seen a consistent pattern of one Minister falling over another, of cancelling one program and replacing it with another without giving any sense of objective or direction as to where the Minister wants to take his or her department or this Government. That mistaken problem of developing any logical or effective economic strategy has once again been high-lighted by the remarks we have just heard from the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) who really is a shimmering mass of contradiction sheathed in a growing sense of his own self-importance.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, it does not add up to what this country is asking for. I think the New Democratic caucus in its

April 16, 1985
Supply
examination, and individual Members of our caucus in their own constituencies, know what Canadians want. People wish this Government well. They did give them a mandate, there is no question about that. People now want this Government to perform. People want to see the results of that performance.
What I want to do in part this afternoon is express those concerns, speaking if I might just for my constituents, those to whom I have spoken during the Easter break. First, they want to know what this Government is trying to achieve. This Government has many Ministers. Let me choose one in particular, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), who has been a great advocate of the idea that the market will solve our problems. That chorus has been echoed time and time again by Conservative Members of Parliament who decry past efforts at public investment job creation and industrial programs that have been attempted to give small businesses in different regions a chance to develop their business prospects and opportunities. "No," they say, "those programs are all wrong. They do not work. We are going to rely upon the market to solve the problems."
What do we have, Mr. Speaker? We have Domtar, we have Petrosar, and we have White. We have the same kind of inconsistency which the Tories were talking about. Where is the market in those cases? I do not know. I guess what happened is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) called in the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, rapped his knuckles and said, "The real market is the political market in Quebec. It is not the economic market that we are concerned about according to our theory." We happen to think that maybe they made the right choice and we should be providing incentives for industry to establish.
But we have a Government preaching theology on the one hand and practising a very different religion on the other. It ends up in a mass of confusion. The Tories do not have an industrial policy. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion time and time again finds himself being contradicted by his boss, just as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) finds himself being contradicted. We need not go through the long history because Members of the House are well aware of the Minister of Finance saying, "We must first take a look at social programs", and the Prime Minister saying, "No, we can't". We remember the Minister of Finance saying, "We are going to provide restraints in these areas of Government programs", and the Prime Minister saying, "No, we can't".
What we have seen up to now is simply Ministers of the Crown bumping into each other, or trying to stay out of each other's way but not producing any clear formula, any clear program, any clear development that will give Canadians some sense of where they are going. That is the fundamental problem we face. We have a Government that came into power without knowing what to do. The Conservatives had their pet theories, but those theories have been abandoned and thrown on the scrap heap. Now they are going from day to day, week to week, changing their minds, changing their programs, and what they end up doing is relying upon previous and past Liberal programs, ones they were so critical about in the
election and which they said did not work. But that is the only source of economic initiative which the Tories have been able to provide so far.
Let me give you another example, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) stands up in this House and lauds the new revolution in job creation, the great sort of Renaissance that we will have in new training activities, except first she cuts back substantially on the amount of money in the programs. With regard to the summer programs for youth, a group of people who rely substantially on federal assistance, with the exception of two provinces every province has had its allocation cut back over last year. When you look at the figures, you see that the young people of this country are being short-changed. No new jobs are being provided.
What about the great promise that the Tories are going to provide career related internships? 1 agree with that because when I saw a Minister I brought that program into being- three years ago. There is nothing new or revolutionary about it. The program has been given a new name. It has been given cosmetic treatment. It offers nothing new in the way of new job creation. The single new initiative by Conservatives for young people has been to cut back the actual expenditure of money for summer youth jobs. That is the only new initiative they have taken for young people. Now we see that the same kind of chicanery is taking place in the so-called Regina manifesto. Approximately $540 million was offered to provide for new training, or new skills development to prepare Canadians for future jobs. However, in the meantime they cancelled the programs which were in place and have not got around to replacing them.
One prime example which illustrates this in a very vivid way was brought to my attention when I met with representatives of the Outreach program in my constituency over the Easter holiday. Their primary job is to help older women to get back into the workforce. They provide employment counselling and job training to enable those who need to return to the workforce to acquire the skills they need to obtain jobs. They showed me a list of potential jobs which were available to those women. What was missing was training for those jobs.
1 asked what had happened because at one time we had the skills growth fund and new training programs. They had been cancelled by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. For some reason or other she did not believe there should be assistance for older women to obtain basic upgrading in skills in order to get into technical training programs. They have been cancelled and nothing has been put in their place. Even though jobs may be available, these older women cannot fill them because this great new revolutionary Government which was to do everything for Canadians has not got around to plugging the holes or filling the vacuums. This vital area of providing training for women who want to get into the workforce is all up in the air. Nothing has been offered.
April 16, 1985

Is that the new kind of economic renewal about which we are talking? They are denying women skills in the workforce. Is this the new Renaissance which the Minister of Employment and Immigration has been promising? I checked further as to why the replacement has not taken place, and I was told that they were consulting again with the provinces, and with everyone else. Consultations have been going on for seven months. I asked when the new program would be ready, and I was told that it may be six or seven months from now. They may be ready to announce the replacements at that point, so we will have lost a full year of opportunity for Canadians to be trained. That does not make sense. That is not effective management; that is not competent Government. That is not providing leadership in the job-creation area. It was simply getting rid of programs because they were "Liberal" programs, but they do not have the wit or ability to manage quickly any replacements so that there will be a continuity of training in the country. I hope Conservative Members of Parliament will be listening to their constituents and taking soundings. That is the reality of what is taking place.
I should like to deal with the great economic conference, when all kinds of people were brought together for consultation. Those people made one mistake. They told the Ministers at the conference something they did not want to hear. They told them that their programs were not working and that the obsessive concentration on deficit reduction would in fact increase unemployment, not help it. The Minister of Finance refused to listen, he just said that they could not be right. Then they brought together 150 of the top corporate leaders, union leaders, educators and community leaders. When these leaders had the honesty to tell it as it was, they were dismissed. The reality is there.
The Hon. Member for Calgary West waxed eloquently about all the prospects. I should like to refer to a report of the Conference Board of Canada, a board which I think Hon. Members of the House agree represents no particular partisan interests. It compiled a report based upon the findings of 18 different private economic forecasters in Canada, everything from banks to university groups and all independent groups in between. What is their forecast for next year and the year after? The growth rate is expected to be 2.8 per cent, possibly closer to 2.2 per cent. This represents a substantial decline from the 4 per cent average growth rate over the past two years. All those policies which were ridiculed and criticized by the Prime Minister and others created a growth rate of 4 per cent over the past two years. The best efforts of this Government, with all the new confidence, motivation and consultation, will result in, according to the 18 best forecasters in Canada, 2.8 per cent at best, and 2.2 per cent at worst. Something is going wrong in the system somewhere.
With that kind of forecast in mind, one would think the Government would start to rethink its position and provide some different judgment on the application of its ideas and principles. We still have this obsessive adherence to a theology with nothing taking its place, no application or implementation of the program. We are now faced with a country in economic
Supply
limbo, a country seized with uncertainty, a country without real economic leadership or direction. We are now heading to a point where there is a down curve on the economic horizon and there is no compass to provide some form of direction. This is why it is important in these debates to put forward the kinds of positions which are necessary and important to create economic growth.
Let me deal with the issue of the fiscal management of the country. I should like to give a word of warning to government Members opposite. As they move toward budget date, and the examination of how they will reduce the deficit, we plead with them to make a simple calculation-any reduction should be based upon jobs gained, not jobs lost. As the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) pointed out earlier today, the end result of the November statement of the Minister of Finance was not a net increase in employment, it was a net decrease in employment. That was the basic problem. We have continually asked the Minister of Finance to show us wrong or to disprove that basic equation. He had refused to do so because he knows we are right. He knows that in fact the end result has been a net reduction in employment, not a net creation of jobs.
The Hon. Member for Calgary West pulled out year over year figures, but he refused or somehow forgot to make the observation that there is also growth in the labour force in those year over year figures. Of course there are changes. There is natural population growth. People come out of school and go into the labour market. We add 200,000 or 300,000 per year to the labour market simply as a result of the number of young people leaving educational institutions. There is a real problem in relation to the basic equation which will be applied to any form of deficit reduction.
Let us take a look at the question of public investment, which I heard the Hon. Member for Calgary West decry, and all its influences. A report of the NDP caucus, based upon a report on which we and the Canadian Federation of Municipalities worked last year, pointed out that there should be a minimum of something like $12 billion of investment in public infrastructure.
The repair of roads, sewers, sewerways, the very basic lifeblood of the country, will need a major infusion of capital over the next five years. Otherwise the ability to gain productivity and to provide for the basic economic cycle to take place will be eliminated.
Helping the railways.

My colleague points out an interesting case. When the Conservatives were in opposition a year ago, along with the New Democrats, they opposed to the very end the Western Grain Transportation Act, which is now putting close to $1.5 billion a year of new capital investment into exactly what the NDP call for; public investment and new infrastructure. There would not be the investment in our railway system in western Canada, which is one of the few stimulants taking

April 16, 1985
Supply
place, if we had not had the courage to bring that in over their opposition. That is the reason there is major capital investment going into that which the NDP is now recommending. But they are a year too late. I wish they had written that report a year ago and that their colleagues at that time could have listened to their good advice.
At the same time, let us talk about the Western Accord. The Hon. Member for Calgary West said it will result in a major change to the economy. When you read the report, the only one to gain will be Texaco, which has the lowest rate of capital investment of any oil company in Canada. The losers will be the very Canadian oil companies which have been investing large sums of capital in energy development over the last four years.
Let's regard this debate as an opening round of the Budget debate. Let's look at it was a warning signal for the Conservatives to try and get their act straight, to forget their theology and, more importantly, to try to put together some coherence in their economic policies so when we get to the Budget on May 20, we will at least know what they stand for and not simply what they stand against.

Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) aware that in the Toronto area the Challenge '85 program introduced by the Minister has led to a situation where private businesses offering career opportunities to young people this summer have over-subscribed the $9 million allotted to the Toronto area. Is he aware that the Department, in co-operation with the Province of Ontario, using the Ontario stimulus fund of $1.25 an hour has created a great number more summer jobs this year than ever before in the past?

Mr. Speaker, I would remind the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) that the original paternity of the seed program was the NEED program which I introduced when I was Minister of Employment and Immigration in 1983. We put $5 million of federal funds forward. With that we attracted an additional $650 million of private sector and provincial funds. The Conservative Government is following a very effective and useful program which was strated by the Liberal Government in 1983, a program which at that time was roundly criticized by the Member himself for not working as well as it should.
I do not object to the notion of using federal job-creation funds as an incentive for private sector and provincial and municipal funds, because that is what I did. That is the program we introduced. It was our Government that put forward the career internship which provided that kind of incentive. What I object to is the way in which the summer youth program has provided major cancellations and restraints
upon a number of community organizations and groups that also have to rely upon summer grants.
You can go from constituency to constituency in this country and find that day care centres, women abuse centres, various forms of social, ethnic and immigration centres cannot get their summer money. I deny the fallacy that their jobs are somehow second rate compared to jobs at a McDonald's restaurant. We should be equally as sensitive about the jobs created for the volunteer sector, the community sector and the service sector. That also gives young people an understanding about the community in which they live. It gives young Canadians an opportunity to develop real skills that we will need in the future to help disadvantaged Canadians, and there will be a lot more disadvantaged Canadians the longer this Government stays in power.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-Fort Garry ought to know that the Challenge '85 program does not provide assistance to McDonald's for serving hamburgers. You might get that kind of assistance from the Province of Ontario job-creation program, but this is a career-oriented program. All sorts of proposals have been turned down because they do not supply enough career instruction and assistance. Even at that, the program is over-subscribed. Surely the Member should stand in his place today and congratulate the Minister for a well-thought-out summer program. As he said, perhaps it follows some of his own thinking.

Mr. Speaker, I would be the first to say that the highest form of flattery is to copy what one has done before. If the Minister is simply copying what the previous Minister of Employment introduced, it shows that at least she is showing good sense in one area of her administration.
I want to provide some correction before the Hon. Member for Mississauga South gets carried away. Every summer program is over-subscribed. Every summer program had three or four times the applications that could be funded. It is nothing new. The fact is that there is always an awful lot more demand than there is supply, which I regret as much as he does. 1 want to know why the supply of money was cut back this year as opposed to being increased, as it naturally should have been.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Win-nipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) referred in his speech to the debate we had when his Government brought forward the legislation to change the Crow rate. He indicated quite correctly that Members of the New Democratic Party had opposed that Bill. At that time, because we opposed it vigorously and kept it from being passed quickly, we were attacked by the Hon. Member, saying that we were holding up the Bill and preventing hundreds of thousands of jobs from being created. I want to ask the Hon. Member what has happened to those thousands of jobs. The Hon. Member knows that in our city, a city which we both represent, as in many other cities, both the CNR and CPR, instead of hiring hundreds or thousands of new workers, have in fact been laying off workers. What happened to those predictions made by the Member who

Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to answer that question, if I may, because the Hon. Member and 1 share constituencies in the same area of Winnipeg. First, I would point out to him that in the past year some 45 new companies made application for assistance to develop new products related to the Western Grain Transportation program. That creates a wide variety of jobs in the private sector. It is being duplicated in western cities and towns right across the three prairie provinces and British Columbia.

The CNR announced 170 layoffs in the Transcona shops because both the federal Conservative Government and the provincial New Democratic Government are not living up to an agreement that we signed a year ago for the construction and rehabilitation of new boxcars in the Transcona shops to provide for running-stock to the Churchill area. Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate on a motion presented by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). That motion states:
That this House calls upon the Government to immediately bring in stimulative proposals to reduce unemployment by a minimum of 2Vi percent within the next 12 months, given the failure of the Government to live up to its commitment to make job creation its number-one priority, and its pursuit, instead, of a policy of cutbacks which has led to a rise in unemployment in three of the last four months.
If we think a national rate of unemployment of 11.2 per cent is rough and tough on Canadians, then let us think about single-industry towns. In single-industry towns, the unemployment rate is much more stifling than 11.2 per cent. There are in excess of 811 single-industry towns across the country.
Earlier I heard the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) talking about the NDP task force. He indicated that when the NDP task force went across the country, perhaps it heard only from people who leaned further to the left than the right. That suggestion was contained in his comments.
I come from a single-industry community. It has been mining from its very inception. We started with forestry, and then after we killed all the forests we set up the mines. Then we smelted close to the ground and the sulphur fumes killed off whatever trees had escaped the woodcutters' saws.
Let me put on record a letter signed by the Chairman of the Regional Municipality of Sudbury. By no stretch of the imagination is he a democratic socialist.
Probably a Conservative.

Well, I would not want to give the Chairman a bad name. Certainly his letter is very poignant and concise. I think it puts this debate in some perspective. The letter is addressed to the Hon. Frank Miller. He writes:
Dear Mr. Premier:
As you are aware, the Regional Municipality of Sudbury continues to suffer the after-effects of the recent recession through a high rate of unemployment, a situation exacerbated by ongoing staff reductions by Inco Limited Falconbridge Limited.
While economic stabilization has been occurring in many other communities across the Province, such is not the case in the Regional Municipality of Sudbury and other Northern communities which depend heavily on a natural resources base. Over the past three years, Sudbury Region has been developing an economic diversification strategy which, in the long-term, we are confident will lead to recovery and eventual new growth.
It is in the short-term that we are experiencing our greatest difficulty. The impact of the recession is manifesting itself in a very serious and rapidly expanding welfare caseload. This not only threatens to severely stifle our economic recovery efforts, but also to substantially increase the Ontario Government's share of the cost of carrying the social welfare burden in our community.
At the peak of the recession, the Region's welfare caseload reached 3,400, which was an all-time high. With the assistance of the CO-ED job-creation programs, we were able to reduce that caseload to 2,300. Had those short-term job creation programs not been available, our caseload could easily have reached

April 16, 1985
Supply
upwards of 4,000. As a result of these dramatic reductions in our welfare caseload, a gross saving of $6.5 million was realized of which the Region's share was $1.3 million.
Because the Region's two major employers, Inco Limited and Falconbridge, provided us with their five-year staff reduction programs, we have been able to forecast the impact on our welfare caseload. Repeatedly, over the past two years, we have been warning your responsible Ministers and their senior staffs of the need to accommodate anticipated welfare caseload increases. Our caseload forecasts are rapidly becoming reality because already we have reached a high level of 3,300 cases, including several hundred young people. In addition, the Region has provided a 1985 budget allocation to accommodate only 2,400 cases during the summer months. It is apparent that the shortfall between available municipal funding and the cost of providing for as many as 900 more cases will produce compounded economic consequences for this community if other alternatives are not available.
We have been informed by both the Federal Government and the Provincial Government that job creation funding will be directed at the private sector. In this community, we cannot understand how this is going to take care of our immediate short-term problem because it is virtually impossible for the private sector in our already depressed economy to create sufficient jobs to pick up the shortfall. Our private sector, exclusive of Inco Limited and Falconbridge Limited which are large multinational corporations, is considerably smaller than in other municipalities of comparable size, and many of these firms produce for and hence depend upon the mining industry.
I think that is relevant, because in single-industry communities there is no private sector. The Government of the day across the way seems to be directing all of its economic energies and incentive programs to the private sector. As I have pointed out, in over 811 single-industry communities there is no extensive private sector. So instead of reducing the unemployment rate it will be exacerbated, as pointed out in the letter written by Mr. Tom Davies, Chairman of the Regional Municipality of Sudbury.
What is it that we can do in the short term to create jobs? I can think of the situation in my own riding. The week before the Easter break, I raised in the House the question of refining resources. It seems absolutely ridiculous that in 1985 resources mined in this country are shipped abroad to be refined outside the borders of Canada. Yet, that is the situation with Falconbridge Nickel Mines. It ships the nickel matte from the Sudbury Basin to Norway, and it has been doing that for the last 40-odd years. It has been shipped to Norway to be refined. However, the International Nickel Company of Canada is not allowed to ship its nickel matte to be refined somewhere else because there is a law in the Province of Ontario.
The Province of Ontario's Mining Act states that resources which are mined in Ontario must be refined in Canada. We would have preferred it to have read "Ontario", but that is fine, it must be refined in Canada. But, Section 104 of the same Act states that it does not apply to Falconbridge Nickel Mines. It seems to me that "a Tory is a Tory is a Tory", and it is a Tory Government which has been running the Province of Ontario for the last 44 years. The Tories wrote the Mining Act.
Hear, hear!

Well, you can applaud, but that kind of leeway which has been given to Falconbridge indicates who really calls the shots in Tory circles. It is not the people who
matter most, it is the rich people who matter most, and preferably the corporations. In fact, we have been after the provincial Tory Government of Ontario to have Falconbridge refine the nickel in the Sudbury Basin.
In the last two years the hourly workforce has been reduced from 2,800 to some 1,700 or 1,800. There were 900 jobs which disappeared. Now comes the denouement. Falconbridge now has an opportunity to buy nickel in Botswana because the AMEX Corporation is pulling out of nickel operations there. So, Falconbridge wants to get a larger share of the world market for nickel and moves into the Botswana market. Falconbridge is taking the Botswana nickel matte and shipping it to Norway to be refined. As a result of that, Falconbridge has to expand the refining capacity in Norway to the tune of $41.5 million Canadian.
It would seem only fair, if this Government is concerned about jobs and the principle that resources should be refined were they are mined, that as a self-respecting Government it should stand by that principle. The Government should tell Falconbridge to build a refinery in the Sudbury Basin to refine Canadian nickel, and to send the scrap to the Falconbridge operation to be smelted. We are not only sending out the matte to be refined in Norway, but we are importing the scrap into Sudbury from which nickel is extracted. That does not create jobs.
The private sector, which the Government worships and bows down to, is not in the business of creating jobs. The private sector is not a manpower centre and is not interested in whether Canadians work. The private sector is interested in what it can get out of the country. The cheaper it can extract to maximize its profits, the more it will do it. We should tell Falconbridge that it cannot do that. The $41.5 million would be a good down payment on a new refinery.
The other day the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), who thought Sudbury was a basement, said that he did not know to what I was referring when 1 asked him a question. He said that he would check with Falconbridge. He did check and sent me a letter. In his letter he said that he checked with Falconbridge and that a new refinery would cost in excess of $200 million and, therefore, the company could not afford to build a new refinery in the Sudbury Basin. However, on April 4, Mr. Peter McBride, who is a spokesman for Falconbridge, said that it would cost at least $125 million to build a Canadian refinery. Well, I would suggest that $41.5 million would be a good down payment on a new refinery. Indeed, I would suggest that both the provincial and federal Governments ought to take equity in the remainder of the $125 million and build a refinery. If that was done, those Governments would have been honest to the principle that resources should be refined where they are mined.
At the rate at which mines are closing today, the Minister of State for Mines will soon be the "Minister without mines".

The mineless Minister.
April 16, 1985

That is right. The Hon. Member said "the mineless Minister". He will lose his car and his chauffeur. We would not want to do that to the Minister.
The Minister said that he understood the plight of Falcon-bridge. He said that the Government does not want to create a regulatory environment which would lead corporations to be unproductive. Well, we in the Sudbury Basin are not asking the Government to create a regulatory environment. We simply want the Government to say to its Tory friends in Ontario: "Remove Section 104 of the Ontario Mining Act and let Falconbridge be subject to the laws of the province and the country".
Not only was 1 a member of the NDP jobs task force, I also toured with my colleagues in northwestern Ontario. We visited communities which were single-industry towns. If one were to look at this on a time span basis, we visited communities which represented the past, the present and the future. We went to Atikokan and saw what happened in the past. We saw our past practices and our past inabilities in dealing with the whole question of single-industry towns, in diversification and job creation. We saw a town in which the mine had run out of ore. The people living in the community in the past had been completely dependent on the mines. Some problems were evident. The fact that the cost of maintaining the services in the municipality fell on fewer shoulders and a more narrow assessment base resulted in home owners having to pay a fantastic cost in order to maintain the infrastructure, let alone putting in new infrastructure. As we went from town to town, that issue arose again and again. We saw a need for a municipal fund from which municipalities could draw, not only to refurbish infrastructure, but to provide improved services to the communities. In my own riding there are still communities where the people cannot drink the water from the well because it is contaminated. People have to drive miles to bring back jars of good water.
We went to other communities. The Griffith mine in Ear Falls is closing after advertising during the previous two years in an effort to attract workers. They put a large advertisement in the newspaper which says in part, "The Griffith mine is a part of this growth, lending a stable economic base to the Red Lake-Ear Falls area with a future that will extend into the 21st century". But last fall it was announced that the Griffith mine is closing and over 700 workers are going to be without work. Just the week before the company convinced several workers to buy the company homes in which they were living and lock themselves into a mortgage.
We recommended that there should be a diversification fund for single industry towns because the local communities are aware of their own needs. Local communities want to have some say in and some control over their economic destiny. In
Supply
fact, the provision of a diversification fund would allow them that flexibility, control and ability to grow and develop and create jobs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion moved by the Opposition certainly reflects their good intentions in emphasizing the need for creating jobs in Canada. However, we intend to make it clear to the House that our hon. friends in the Opposition have completely lost touch with reality.
Mr. Speaker, in our Agenda for Economic Renewal tabled last November, we set forth the strategy to be followed in three key areas namely, first of all, limiting and ultimately reversing the massive build-up in public debt; second, redefining the role of government so that it provides a better framework for growth and job creation and less of an obstacle to change and innovation; and third, adopting policies that foster greater

April 16, 1985
Supply
innovation, increased international competitiveness and a positive climate for the birth and growth of new enterprise. Without this kind of strategy, Canada as it is today will not be able to sustain durable economic growth that will create jobs.
I shall, if 1 may, review each of these points. The rising deficit and our cumulative debt are a serious threat to economic growth and renewal. It is not so much a matter of ideology as simply recognizing the very serious problem caused by the disastrous effect of compound interest on the national debt. Gaining absolute control over the deficit is not an end in itself, but it is the only way we can achieve our objective to create jobs and sustainable growth. That is why this Government announced last November that putting its fiscal house in order would be the first item on its agenda for economic renewal. It is also why we have quickly taken steps to control public spending effectively and efficiently.
We believe that if we are to control the deficit, our priority must be to reduce Government spending, which implies more efficient management of Government programs. Improving efficiency of management practices in our public administration is essential, but this alone will not resolve the problems created by the deficit. We will have to examine existing programs and carefully scrutinize Government spending, but nevertheless, total expenditures are so high compared with Government revenues, that even if every possible measure is taken to reduce spending, the deficit and cumulative debt may continue to be a problem. Although necessary to ensure economic growth, controlling the deficit alone is not enough. That is why we said last November that two other elements were equally important if we were to achieve our goal of creating jobs and sustainable growth.
The second requirement is to redefine the role of Government so that it becomes less of an obstacle to growth. An intricate web of regulations, subsidies and other forms of intervention has built up over the years. What seemed to be straightforward protective measures at the time have now become, in many cases, an economic straight-jacket. This network of Government intervention has created a major obstacle to growth-more diffuse, less easy to measure and quantify but every bit as real as our present financial problems.
We are trying gradually to remove these obstacles in order to be able to establish a framework of policies that will promote the creation of jobs and economic growth.
Mr. Speaker, the Members of the Opposition would like us to act quickly and do the exact opposite of what we are doing now. Our answer is simple. We have been quick to intervene in a number of areas. In other areas, however, we have not yet done so because it is very important to attain a better understanding of available options and to establish a better basis for co-operation, so that when we do make our decisions, they will produce the best possible results.
To this end, the Government has developed a very specific program, and we are ready and determined to act: first of all, to promote healthy competitiveness by adopting updated competition legislation; to relieve small businesses of their unproductive administrative paper burden; to simplify regulations for transport, communications, and financial services. In this
connection, I might remind the House that yesterday, the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) released in Montreal a discussion paper that is intended to pave the way for the first major revisions in decades to the regulations governing financial institutions; to update our copyright and patent legislation; to simplify our tax system; to streamline our system for providing grants to industry; to remove obstacles to investment; to free the oil and gas industry from the restrictions of extreme regulation and taxation; and to reform many other areas of public policy.
We are resolved to deal with these issues and with many others, but without undue haste, so as to be sure to succeed on our first try, something some members of the Opposition do not seem to understand, Mr. Speaker.
We must do a lot more than just redefining the role of government and removing obstacles to growth. We must act to foster a positive climate for investment, innovation, and increased international competitiveness. That is the third aspect of our strategy for economic renewal.
Allow me to explain where we are focussing our efforts. Suppose we consider investment. If we want to promote sustained economic growth, we must encourage investment in new production areas that will create jobs. The energy sector has a major role to play in economic renewal, and growth in this industry will resume if we go back to a pricing system determined by market conditions, if we go back to more realistic and sounder tax incentives and if we remove the burden of regulations. We feel that a strong and expanding energy sector is essential to our national economy, not only to ensure security of our oil supplies and not just because the energy sector represents 30 per cent of total private investment, but also because it constitutes a major customer for businesses, both large and small, in all regions of this country.
Let us consider external trade. Guaranteed access to foreign markets is another essential element of any realistic economic recovery strategy. A number of reasons justify such a statement, the most obvious being the fact that millions of Canadian men and women are now employed in industries ranging from forestry to car manufacturing, and that they would not be working if there were no foreign markets. In turn, those jobs create others so that Canadians can respond to the needs of our exporters.
In other words, external trade creates jobs, and losing access to foreign markets means fewer jobs. It is as simple as that.
April 16, 1985

But that is not the only factor to consider. Guaranteed market access is a must if we want to compete on the international scene, as it is for creating economies of scale and competitive specializations, and for the kind of industrial adjustments that will enable us to boost our exports while at the same time coping more easily with competitive imports here in Canada. A major factor to consider before deciding to build a plant is whether or not foreign markets are readily available.
It is a decisive factor in attracting job-creating foreign investments and making sure that our national companies can expand from their Canadian base.
New technology also offers opportunities to produce new goods and services and create jobs, but above all it will protect many other jobs in existing industries through higher productivity. New technology ought to be considered as a powerful tool which will help us improve our competitiveness on international markets.
What we mean is this: it is important to develop high technology, and even more so to use that technology in traditional industries such as textiles and clothing, forestry and mining, car manufacturing, and particularly the steel industry.
That is why we put so much emphasis on research and development, just as we do on the adoption, use and expansion of the best technology available. We believe that to be crucial if we are to remain competitive and raise our standard of living.
If we want to make the best of technology, we must train and recycle young and middle-aged Canadian men and women and teach them how to use those new tools. We must also be resigned to the fact that technological advance will force some Canadian workers to keep up with this evolution. It is a fact we cannot ignore, or else we might stand to lose even more existing jobs. The workers themselves have a major role to play in coping with this evolution. We must make sure that, besides providing support income for those whose needs are temporary, our programs are consistent with the training and mobility of workers facing a bleak outlook. The answer is to give them opportunities to develop new skills and encourage workers to take a chance by seeking employment in other fields or moving to other regions.
To clear up all possible misunderstanding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that it is important not only to create jobs that provide Canadian men and women with the major means to get their share of the wealth within the Canadian society, but it is equally important to create the wealth which Canadian men and women can share through a whole range of services, including a social security system, the purpose of which is to help those who need them and cannot provide for themselves.
These are areas which are given very high priority by our government, Mr. Speaker. We have been working on them
Supply
ever since last September, but there are no miracle cures to our economic woes, no short cuts toward creating jobs and wealth. Canadians are aware that if prosperity were the result of spending and indebtedness, it would have been ours a long time ago. But such is not the case, and we will have to work still harder and more intelligently to achieve our growth potential, a healthy and lasting growth which will help us create new jobs for all Canadian men and women who are anxious to work.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the somewhat intellectual discourse of the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) whom I have often seen walking along corridors while reading impressive-looking documents. Mr. Speaker, I would like to pose some questions with reference to the deficit. The Hon. Member has spoken in customary Conservative tones with respect to this issue, as befits a Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. However, I want to ask if he would be prepared to concede that, just as we would have predicted, by trying to focus on the deficit, making it a preoccupation, we have in fact seen an increase in the deficit in this country since this Government has taken power. Secondly, would he be prepared to confirm, given the intellectual approach that was suggested, that there are of course other ways to control deficits besides reducing expenditures? For example, by increasing taxes and acting on the suggestions of our task force report, that it be no longer possible for companies to deduct the interest expense involved in taking over other companies, something the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself talked about at the National Economic Conference. Does he not agree that it would be a good idea for companies that have large amounts of deferred taxation to pay interest on it? Does he not agree that these too would contribute to concern about the deficit and permit the extra expenditures which would give us the jobs we need in the country? Finally, would the Member not agree that if we decreased interest rates by two to three percentage points that too would have a significant impact on the deficit in the country?
We have had varied estimates. One economist at the University of British Columbia suggested that there would be a saving of $1 billion in the deficit for each decrease of a single point in the interest rate. I myself think that is probably an over-estimate because bonds will be due in different years. At the very least, bringing interest rates down two to three percentages points would save $600 million to $900 million. That is the estimate within our report. Surely the Member would agree that all of this would give us much greater capacity to be making the essential expenditures to provide encouragement to private investment that would increase jobs in the country.
