Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate today on the motion presented by our New Democratic Party colleagues. First, I would like to talk about the unemployment situation in my riding. I had hoped that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) would hear what we are saying today, so that acting on behalf of his Minister, he could create some jobs in my riding. But he is no longer with us-and I am not saying he is away from the House because that would be out of order-but let us say that I would have liked to have seen him here.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, the riding or rather part of the riding 1 represent, namely Prescott, which most of the Members of this House living in the East have had occasion to cross in travelling to their ridings-Prescott has 1,686 unemployed. That is a very high unemployment rate, and it has been for some time, increasing all the while. I can assure the House that the people in my riding who saw the results on election day remembered this Government's promises and expected the Government to create new jobs. They are still waiting, Mr. Speaker. This Government was elected eight months ago, and there has not been a single new job in my riding. In fact, there are fewer jobs now than there were on election day iast year.

Before the Government was elected it made several promises to the Canadian people. 1 have referred to them before on occasion in the House. We have put together a document


April 16, 1985

called "338 Tory Promises". I will read a few of them regarding employment, particularly unemployment amongst our youth.
During the election campaign the Government told us how it would streamline government programs and make them efficient. The most innnovative thing they could do last winter was to use some of the Canada Works Programs of the previous Government, which they had chastised before. That is not very innovative. If the programs were not good enough while they were in Opposition, one would wonder why they are all of a sudden good enough when they are in Government. Although they had only been in power for about three months, they had claimed for a few years that they were ready to take over. However, they could not organize a better winter works program. They simply used the program which was in place before, always claiming that it was no good to start with.
With regard to young people, Mr. Speaker, you will remember that the Government said it would scrap the Liberal program for youth summer employment because they felt it was not adequate and they would have a better one. Months passed, Mr. Speaker. Many people phoned their Members of Parliament asking about the youth program Challenge '85. The forms for that program were distributed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). A little kit was sent to all Members of Parliament. The first thing I did when I got that kit was phone the Minister's office to ask for 150 application forms to give to businesses in my riding. After all, the least we could do was try to make this program work, notwithstanding the fact that it was started too late and was poorly organized.
The Minister's office said that they could not give me forms. I asked why and was told that they did not have them but that they would be at the Canada Employment centres. I argued that. I came into the House and talked to the Minister personally. Lo and behold, when I went back to my office a couple of hours later there were all kinds of forms. There was a stack of them about an inch thick, or 2.54 centimetres if you wish.
I brought those forms to my constituency office and my constituents used them and sent them to the Government. The Government then said they were the wrong forms. Do you believe this? The Minister sent them to my office and they were the wrong forms. A couple of weeks later we got new forms from the Minister. The program was supposed to end at the end of March and it was March 20 when we got the forms. There were only a few days left for all employers to apply. If the Government did not intentionally try to sabotage this program, it certainly did a very good accidental job of achieving that result.
It is now mid-April. Today businesses from my riding were contacting me asking whether I had any news about the Challenge '85 applications which they had submitted. There is nothing I can tell them. Our young people are finishing school now. Other programs are starting. They do not know whether they will be accepted by this program. They do not know whether the youth will be going to work elsewhere. They are

not sure what to do. They are waiting and we cannot get any answers.
This is not the fault of the people at the various Canada Employment centres. They did their best to make this thing work. It was so poorly designed and started so late that it was almost impossible for it to work. I cannot help but wonder how the staff working for the department managed to do anything at all. It must be very difficult for them, and I know they are working very hard, but it is impossible.
What the Government has failed to recognize is that it should have kept the previous program that was in place, made it work. When the Government was ready for a change and it had designed a new program it should have introduced it then. I recognize that the Government has the right to do what it did, it is the Government after all, but you do not cancel something and then think later of maybe doing something else. First you find alternatives and then you change. You do not do the reverse. That logic is something you would understand, Mr. Speaker, but obviously not this Conservative Government. That kind of logic has escaped this Government.
Let us review some of the promises the Government has made to young people in this 338-promise document to which I referred a while ago, Mr. Speaker. This Government made lots of promises to our youth. It was trying to get young people to knock on doors and canvass. This Government promised everything to the youth. Under youth employment, it said, "encourage young people to remain in school, ensure training components in all job creation programs, provide incentives to encourage private sector training programs, the utilization of UIC benefits for training purposes, and encourage local training councils." These councils would identify training needs and co-ordinate training programs, establish a refundable employer tax credit for employers to hire and train young people for specific periods of time.
There are 12 promises here for our young people. As far as I can see, none of them have been adopted by this Government and it is now eight months after the election. This Government has yet to fulfil one promise to our young people. It must be very disheartening. I see one Member saying to me, "Yes, we did". I do not know, perhaps this Government has appointed a person on another board that I have not heard about and that constitutes a job creation program to which the Hon. Member is referring. But this is not good enough for the rest of the young people who are waiting for a real meaningful effort on the part of their Government.
This Government when elected claimed it was ready to take over, ready to run the country. I see some Conservative Members in this House, the ones sitting at the edges on this side, what we refer to as the "book-ends" or the "surfers". Surfers means they were elected with the tide and they will go out with the tide in three years' time. The book-ends in this House are nodding in agreement that this Government was ready to take over. Why is it that this is the longest period of time after an election in the history of this country without a

budget? Is that synonymous with good government, Mr. Speaker, a Government that cannot even present its financial package to the House of Commons eight months after coming into office? Not only that, but we will have to wait another month before we get the budget.
There happens to be in the intervening month an Ontario election. Some of us say that it is a mere coincidence that an Ontario election is looming. The Tories in Ontario are not doing so well. Their popularity is going down daily. That popularity will go down a lot more before the election, and we will have the election of the next Liberal provincial government. The popularity of the Provincial Tories is going down. They know they have a noose down around their necks in the person of the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson.) He will impose on the people of Canada major taxation increases and present a disastrous budget immediately after the Ontario provincial election. Then, Mr. Speaker, you can understand why it was that the Premier of Ontario paid a visit to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and that this visit had two purposes. One was to object that he had not been consulted on the western oil deal, and second, to ensure that under no circumstances would we see a federal budget before that election. As bad as the Tories are doing now provincially, they would have done worse later because of the disastrous budget we have coming. 1 am sure you, Mr. Speaker, being the nonpartisan person that you are, would understand this, although your colleagues obviously do not.
Hon. Members will remember that on November 8, 1984, the Minister of Finance introduced his program known as the Expenditure Review. This Expenditure Review program, commonly known as the "Black Thursday Program", was a program of cut-backs. Many of these cut-backs were in the area of employment. Hon. Members will recall that a little earlier I asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) how does one create employment by cutting jobs. He took notice of the question. He did not answer it.
Let me review some of the employment creation initiatives that were cut-back by the same people who said they were going to create jobs. The Employment Assistance Entitlement Program had a $200 million cut back. Let us see what this program did. The Unemployment Insurance Act provided for the establishment of an employment services program and this program was cut back. This service is now gone. The unemployment insurance payments have been cut back by $5.8 million; the mobility program was cut by $2.8 million. Let me speak briefly about mobility grants.
I have a constituent who is in Alberta at the present time. He left two or three years ago and went to work out there, but now he does not have a job. He has a job offer here in the City of Ottawa which he could take immediately. Because these mobility grants have been curtailed severely, he cannot take up this job in Ottawa. The unemployment insurance people told him that once he has exhausted his unemployment insurance benefits then they would pay him to move. If you can understand the logic of this, Mr. Speaker, I am glad. Under these new rules my constituent will have to be on unemployment for
about eight months drawing money out of the federal treasury before we give him money to come back here to a job he could have today if we were to allow him to come back. If that logic escapes you, Mr. Speaker, you are not the only one. It escapes me as well, and it escapes my constituent. Seemingly that makes sense to the Minister of Finance. Perhaps to no one else, but to him it does. To make someone draw eight months more of unemployment insurance benefit before paying the mobility grant that he could be given today, seeing that he has a job promised is the policy of this Government toward creating employment, and I do not understand it. It is small wonder that this program is not working.
On November 8, the Minister of Finance introduced that program of cut-backs to which I referred earlier and which 1 described as the "Black Thursday Program". I see that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) is here. He will recall this document that was given to Cabinet Ministers which contains the answers they were supposed to give to journalists when interviewed about the cut-backs. There were questions on the census but they have become redundant now because the census has been reinstated, as we know. I applaud the Minister for that. I know he wanted it all along. He was only trying to twist the arm of the Minister of Finance. Obviously he managed to swing it, and I am glad he did.
However, I should like to read some of the questions and answers on employment. The following was a tentative question which someone in the press was supposed to ask the Minister:
Why is employment pension income considered as earned income when eligibility for unemployment insurance is determined?
The Minister was supposed to answer as follows:
Changes in the UI program, which will result in pension income arising from employment being deducted from UI benefits, will eliminate double payments and reinforce the concept that UI is an income replacement scheme.
That is the only reason many people in the country, including military personnel and others, contributed to unemployment insurance. Otherwise they would have no possibility of collecting it. Obviously what we should do now is refund their premiums from the beginning in that we have made them join a program from which they could not benefit.
Another tentative question reads:
Whal is the object of the changes in the Employment Assistance and Entitlement Program?
The Minister is supposed to answer as follows:
A strengthened interview program for all claimants on regular benefits will better determine their needs for employment services.
Now I know from where the Minister of Employment picked up this line when she referred to it in the House. The Minister of Finance had given it to her in a briefing book. She was supposed to say it to the public. That is ridiculous. The answer given by the Minister got her no place.
In conclusion, our Party is very much dissatisfied with the efforts of this Government in creating employment.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House, authored by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), suggests that unemployment should be lowered by 2.5 per cent and that the Government should commit itself to that goal. It is natural, given the content of the resolution, that reference should be made to the recently released report of the New Democratic Party task force on jobs. One might have hoped that the discussion would have been a constructive and informed one.
One was inevitably disappointed to discover that as usual the debate turned, not upon the content of the resolution, the content of the report or the exercise that resulted in its production. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) stood before us and told us that the report of the New Democratic Party job action group was constructive, interesting, had some good suggestions, and then proceeded to criticize it, not on the basis of its content, but on press report after press report. It soon became clear that that was the only source of information to which she could refer.
That should not have been particularly surprising. The Minister of Employment and Immigration knew almost as much about her Challenge '85 student summer employment program as she did about the task force report. She insists on reiterating what she said when the program was announced. She said it will be based on wage subsidized career-oriented jobs which will prepare students for the work world.
The fact is that although she claims there are larger numbers of applications than there were previously, the criteria that would have produced the kinds of jobs that she was going to achieve were not being applied. The fact is that no applications involving fewer than four student employees is being subjected to any test of whether or not the jobs are career oriented. That is fine.
In the sense that jobs are created, and the Minister reverted to a few standards, indeed reverted to standards which are less rigorous than Summer Canada, her claim that more jobs are being created may in fact be correct. Many of us who would have expected her to achieve the goals she indicated thought she would have attempted to ensure that there was some measure of career orientation, that permanent jobs were not being lost, that the career content of those jobs would be supervised to ensure their achievement during the period of employment. We were also concerned about the fact that in contrast to Summer Canada of last year, there is no affirmative action portion, in spite of Government commitments to the contrary, which would have assured reasonable participation by natives, women, visible minorities and ethnic groups.
We heard the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), who was similarly well informed about the document, insisting that the document surely had to be the result of going from city to city across this country, some 24 of them, and speaking only to supporters of the New Democratic Party. It was kind of exciting news, at least to this Member, to discover that the Canadian Automobile Parts Manufacturers, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, association of small businesses, and women's organizations all across this country support not the Liberals or the Conservatives, but the New Democratic Party. Similarly, small woodlot owners, industry associations, forest industry associations are all suddenly New Democratic Party supporters. Of course that is nonsense. There was no discrimination in the selection of those who appeared before us.
There was one thing that came out of the whole exercise loud and clear. It was that the priority of this House should be the creation of jobs. Some Members opposite will remember when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that "we are going to see tens of thousands of jobs being created just as quickly as the new Government is sworn in". He has encountered some impediments. We decided to take him at his word, his word having been that he, in spite of his Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and others on that side of the House, was interested in job creation. If one refers to some of the statements made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign, he will see that the Prime Minister said that we are going to get local communities and small business more involved in job creation. This is going to be accomplished by a program of community self-help which will be launched through the establishment of the Canada Opportunity Development Board. But it should be noted that he did not say exactly what this board would do. There are 70 recommendations in this report which specify what such kinds of community economic development boards might do and how they might be encouraged by the Government.
We should pause for just a moment to consider some of the other criticisms which we have heard from across the way. We have heard that the New Democratic Party proposes that all of the solutions to employment must be achieved by direct government investments, the implication being the take-over of industry and everything else. I would suggest that Members opposite look at the report. They will find that there is very little relationship to that stereotype. What we have attempted to do is to present to the Government some suggestions by which it might approach the goal that the Prime Minister indicated he was attempting to achieve.
The issue of job creation has been laid aside by and large in an effort to combat the deficit, as if knocking down or cutting the deficit were not only an economic imperative but a moral imperative. It is kind of interesting to hear the rhetoric of the deficit cutters. I suppose that many of them have not noticed that this kind of commitment, which has been cited as having been made in British Columbia, has failed. Indeed, it has increased the amount of unemployment, cut the number of jobs and placed a number of businesses in serious difficulty. On the contrary, in Manitoba, where the converse approach was taken, jobs were created.
April 16, 1985

If one looks at various western nations which have attempted to solve their economic problems by using the cutting of the deficit as a target, he will see that they too have failed. On the contrary, one should look at the very interesting Canadian experience during World War II where the deficit achieved levels amounting to 21 per cent of Gross National Expenditures and averaged some 17 per cent of the GNE for a three-year period, yet the rate of unemployment was cut from 11.2 per cent to about 1 per cent and the deficit was wiped out in about three years.
Members may consider that this is irrelevant, that it is a question of expenditures for wartime. However, it is interesting to note that those who preach supply side economics are completely unconscious of the fact that products will not be bought by unemployed consumers. In the United States, where supply side economics and deficit cutting has been preached, indeed preached from the pulpit, deficits have accumulated on the basis of military expenditures, and this has indeed resulted in jobs and economic growth. Canadians across this land fear that our new dependency on the United States will hook us to the philosophy sometimes articulated in this Chamber that we can create jobs by increased military expenditures, by becoming starry-eyed about star wars.
There is one thing we have found across this country that should be clearly enunciated here. In spite of the high rates of unemployment and a deep sense of concern about the future of families, young people and people of all ages, Canadians have become convinced, and we heard this from one ocean to the other, that this country has the resources. It has the human talent to determine its own economic future and to create jobs without turning beyond our borders for help. Just as we do not want to look to Washington or New York for the solutions to our problems in respect to economic growth and job creation, so too do the regions reject the notion that the solution to our ecnomic difficulties and job-creation problems is to be found in the centralized bureaucracy not only of government but of the exploitative profit making of large corporations.
There is nowhere in this report where the New Democratic Party proposes to reject the involvement of large corporations and businesses in job creation. However, it does insist that whether they be a domestic or foreign company, they be obliged to fulfil the needs of Canadians with respect to job creation, increased exports, increased research and development and all of those things which are necessary for the creation of jobs in this country.
To return to the statement by the Prime Minister indicating that he looked to creating community development agencies, I wish Members opposite would read the report because there are constructive suggestions contained therein, the common thread of which is shared by people all across the country. We do have the resources. We are tired of having those resources exploited by others for the benefit of others while we in our regions and communities suffer job losses. We know that the forests, the fisheries, the agricultural sector and any of our
Supply
natural resources have the potential through secondary manufacturing to create jobs, the kinds of jobs we in the local regions understand best. Those sectors can give us the wherewithal by which to do it.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration stood before us supposedly discussing this document and said that they are going to do all kinds of new things with respect to training, retraining, preparing young people for jobs and preparing older people for the necessity of adapting to new jobs. That is fine. However, it is insufficient in the magnitude in which she has proposed it because it only addresses part of the report. There is not much sense in training or retraining people if the jobs are not there.
There now exists considerable literature on how municipal Governments in co-operation with other sectors of the community can engage in analyses of the advantages and disadvantages of the resources, both human and otherwise, that are available, and to engage in long-term planning so that priorities can be established which will allow the growth of co-operatives, small businesses and means by which jobs can be produced based upon the resources possessed by the local communities. When we talk of a government expenditure of $850 million for community development incentives, we are not talking about spreading money around, we are talking at least in part about providing communities not only with the means of financing by with tax changes which will encourage local investment and will provide the kind of expert help that is often needed in order for communities to engage in these activities.
The Federation of Canadian Municipalities recognizes the merit of this approach. I would advise Members opposite to read the report of the New Democratic Party and to read the recommendations of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. If they did so, they would realize that with a very small increase in the deficit, jobs can be created with increased emphasis on local initiatives and less dependency on megaprojects.
We have been told that Members of the New Democratic Party have suddenly realized the problems associated with deficits. I do not know where in the world this attitude arose, but I will say that if the recommendations of our report were followed, the amount of deficit that would be accumulated would be no greater than the tax forgivenesses obtained by the oil companies as a result of the Western Accord, and there would be the production of far more jobs.
I hope that over the coming weeks members of the government Party and of the Official Opposition will engage in a very carefully reading of our document. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which is before the House now and which I must try to deal with is nothing more than a piece of rhetoric on the part of the New Democratic Party, which calls upon the Government to bring in immediately stimulative proposals to reduce unemployment by 2Vi per cent within the next 12 months, and blames the Government for not living up to its commitment to make job creation its number one priority.
On the other hand, we know that this motion is intended as the end result, the crowning piece of the famous report which a group of members of that party brought forth following their visit through various parts of the country in an effort to get support for their ideas, judging from media reports both during and after their tour. With what result? I do not intend to play politics with that, Mr. Speaker. I will merely quote from what was reported in the papers. For instance, here is a Canadian Press article signed by Eric Courchesne which stated that their report was merely an extension of the NDP platform, and 1 quote:

"its recommendations are in large part an expansion of earlier NDP proposals".

Anthony Westell, a Toronto Star columnist, has written that the NDP task force, "having started as a lion in January to solve the unemployment problem, has given birth to a mouse in April". In addition, Carol Goar of The Toronto Star has recorded a diversion in NDP philosophy, as others have, when she wrote on April 11 that "the New Democrats, after promoting for at least two decades a vigorous centralizing strategy" have been getting throughout the country "a signal telling them that interventions must obtain at the local and municipal levels".
By the way, Mr. Speaker, this is what this Government has promoted and accomplished through a policy which I will discuss later on and which is based on a more practical cooperation with other levels of government and the private sector.
On the evening the NDP report was published, we heard similar comments on television. For instance, Robert Duffy said that the report contained-

"pretty traditional ideas. It sounded like the conservative ideas about the deficit".

Indeed, many analysts have pointed out that the New Democrats were no longer in favour of an unrestrained deficit, and as noted in The Toronto Star:

"backed away from the traditional NDP position that much bigger government deficits are needed to curb unemployment".

In other words, they agree to a deficit, but not necessarily to an overly large deficit.
Then again columnist Don McGillivy has written that: [English]
"the action group's report is fairly confused and confusing on what should be done to create jobs".
Mr. Speaker, that report was published on April 10, and it carried so much interest that it was a mere five days later, on April 15, that the Journal de Montreal paid any attention to it in an article entitled:
The NDP proposes the creation of 300,000 jobs.
Yes, five days later. In addition, on April 15, the newspaper Le Devoir also had an article on this important report which said, and I quote:
-announced last week.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, that new report was readily recognized as being old hat and its authors acknowledged that a centralizing policy of unrestrained expenditures with no thought being given to the deficit was no longer saleable. On the other hand, as the Minister of Employment and Immigration said during the debate this morning, the New Democrats must still be congratulated on having admitted that their policies could go no further, or at least not as far as they had suggested until then, in other words on having recognized the effectiveness of this Government's initiatives.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the strategy of this Government, which 1 shall now discuss, is not the perfect solution for, in a world where every country is faced with unemployment problems, if there were any magic solution, it would already have been found and implemented. However, there are alternate options, and it is in support of these options that the
April 16, 1985

Canadian people expressed their views last September, and it is also what has guided the policy of this Government since then, both in the economic statement made by the Minister of Finance on November 8 and in the many consultations undertaken by a great number of Ministers, such as the Minister of Employment and Immigration, before the new strategy was announced at the Federal-Provincial Conference in Regina and the National Economic Conference held here in Ottawa a few weeks ago.
One of the Government's objectives has been to launch a national dialogue and restore-especially in the private sector, which is the driving force of our economy-a climate of confidence designed to promote the establishment of new industries and the expansion or reorientation of many others already in operation. This has been the purpose of the initiatives I have just referred to, and of the new orientations with which 1 am more familiar in my current responsibilities as Parliamentary Secretary, namely job creation and manpower training, whereas more emphasis has been laid on practical training, practical jobs, and closer coordination between the provincial and federal Governments and the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, the employment outlook is already much brighter, a fact which was confirmed a few days ago in Montreal when I attended the seminar of an association of college and university employment whose role, as Hon. Members know, is to make it easier for university and college graduates to join the labour market. I was told that this year more graduates will be able to land jobs in their own field of specialization and that chances are better that those jobs will turn out to be permanent.
Employers have regained confidence in the future of our national economy, and so have workers who are rejoining the labour market in ever increasing numbers. The over-all employment statistics reflect that encouraging trend, but the main point is that such a change in attitude can only contribute to make the situation even better.
With respect to manpower training and job creation, the Government has made a special effort to simplify programs, a sector which has been highlighted by the new labour market development strategy, while much duplication has been eliminated, with the result that we are getting better cooperation from the provinces, including Quebec, as everybody knows.
New formulas have also been designed so that the programs will be more readily accessible to all Canadians, including some people who need special assistance such as, for example, the handicapped, native people, and others who are often called quitters or drop-outs. I would be remiss if I failed to mention in passing that the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced a few weeks ago an employment equality program which was unanimously greeted as a historic step in the evolution of the status of women in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the new labour market development strategy is clearly geared to future manpower requirements in Canada,
Supply
yet it does take into consideration the current technological revolution which is changing our lives at an ever accelerating rate.
In addition, instead of being designed for the short term-if that were so, as was the practice until now, the workers would not be getting anywhere-most of our programs will henceforth be extended over many years so as to ensure better coordination and greater practical efficiency.
The Challenge '85 Program for the benefit of young people this summer was given a more practical approach particularly to provide them with jobs along the line of the careers they have chosen. We also know that the private sector will play a greater role in it and recent figures provided this morning by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) on results attained so far indicate that the program is understood-that there are people who do not even understand the formulas is beyond me-supported and, despite the concerns expressed in some circles, will succeed far beyond initial expectations. Again, the co-operation not only with private enterprise but with the provinces and municipalities has been beneficial. The young are more confident and I repeat that I was able to see that for myself when I recently attended the convention of the University and College Placement Association held in Montreal on March 28 last.
If time allows, Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate on what six main bases lies the new labour market development strategy that the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced at the recent federal-provincial conference in Regina. The first allotment of $80 million was earmarked for manpower training. The second allotment of $350 million for employment development is designed to help people who have been without work for a long time and need retraining to land a job.
In that respect, the Minister of Employment and Immigration pointed out last March 19 that these new programs will have to meet the needs of the regions, be flexible, and call for community participation. The Government and the private sector must share responsibilities. On March 19, the Minister also stressed the fact that small business must play a leading role. Mr. Speaker, there is the third allotment of $125 million for vocational integration. Those are programs for youths who are school drop-outs and unable to find employment, as well as for a great number of women who want to join the labour force for the first time.
These programs are aimed at specific groups and have been set up with the co-operation of the provinces. They feature counselling, training and actual job experience. They are also designed to help the handicapped, native people and other underprivileged groups.
The fourth part is a $40 million program for the development of communities, to assist towns and cities whose economy is often based on one or two industries in trouble or even forced out of business. Obviously, co-operation is essential in that area not only between senior governments but also with

April 16, 1985
Supply
the municipalities and industries concerned. All federal departments which could provide some assistance are also involved.
Fifthly, Mr. Speaker, innovation will be encouraged through a program with a budget of $100 million during the 1985-86 fiscal year to stimulate innovation in the labour market through new pilot projects and new undertakings in the private sector. This also includes the re-entry of women on the labour market, the alternance between work and education and pilot projects for the restructuration of working conditions.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, before concluding, the sixth part of the new strategy for the development of the labour market will have at its disposal $65 million to eliminate any manpower shortage. Indeed, in spite of the high rate of unemployment, some employers are looking desperately for qualified workers. This program is aimed at improving prospects concerning future needs of the private sector and to make sure that employers hire more women.
Before concluding, if you allow me to borrow terms usually used by grammarians, I would say that we did not go from the imperfect to past perfect, but we have surely made some improvements.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions or comments? Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, the motion we have before us today deals with a very important matter, the joblessness people are still experiencing in Canada despite all the promises we had in the last election. I was part of the jobs action group of the NDP and many of the proposals brought forward by my colleagues today came out of the consultations we had in a large number of communities from coast to coast. We started in St. John's, Newfoundland, where unemployment is very high, and went right across to Vancouver Island on the West Coast. Since I have a very short time left to me, let me just highlight some of the very constructive proposals which came from these communities for creatively working at dealing with the unemployment rate and making job creation a priority of the Government instead of slashing programs.
These communities told us they wanted local initiatives. They wanted producer co-ops and community development in their own communities controlled by them. They told us they were tired of having multinational corporations coming into their communities, extracting resources, making money and leaving. We heard this all across Canada. As a result, one of the proposals was that there be special funds available for community initiatives, ensure that co-ops and community development and not government corporations qualify for existing business assistance. The report suggests that there be reduced tax rates on community initiatives, that there be marketing and financial management assistance, and that employees in communities have the right of first refusal to purchase the assets of a company which would otherwise be shutting down. In that way they could keep the company going and see that the profits get ploughed back into the community.
It suggests that the federal Government itself give its business to credit unions and caisses populaires which are prepared to finance community projects. This is a way of putting our own public money into businesses which will aid other businesses.
We should see that a community diversification fund is established, funded by profits made in single industry towns by the corporations, so that the community would not be struck dead when the plant has a shutdown, temporary or long term. There should be an extension of tax credits, like political tax credits, to individuals who donate to voluntary and charitable organizations which produce new jobs. These are constructive and important proposals and we wish the Government would listen and include them in the Budget will be coming down next month.
Another important point made to us by communities hit by unemployment came from women's groups because they are still hit harder by unemployment than men, and when they are working, are still earning less money. One of the important points these groups made is that the service jobs which have expanded enormously in the last decade, jobs in education, health care and child care, have been cut back through federal and provincial Government so called restraint programs. This is something I think a Conservative Government really has to pay attention to. The ideological blinders the Conservatives wear keep them from developing public sector jobs because of their preference for the public sector, regardless of the cost in jobs or to women. These are good jobs which mean improvement in the quality of life for Canadians. We are not just talking about jobs for the sake of jobs but jobs which will actually improve the way Canadians live. These jobs have been very important for women who have improved their chances enormously in the last decade through the expansion of this sector, and they are the people who are hit by the compressions budgetaires in this sector.
Finally, I would like to point to the youth initiative fund we have proposed. While a tenth of adults are unemployed, a fifth of young people are unemployed in Canada. This is shocking. Young people coming out of school can look to long periods of job search, and often not end up with jobs at all. We have proposed a youth initiative fund, initially at $600 million, for new initiatives in community and social services, energy conservation, environmental protection and arts and culture. This would produce some 40,000 new jobs, an important and constructive proposal.
Let me also, as the arts and culture critic for the NDP caucus, say that we heard from arts and culture groups. This part of the economy has an enormous job potential. It is growing, and even with cutbacks in Government funding over the last decade more people have been going into arts and culture because the audience is there and Canadians want to see expansion in this area. It is a simple fact that for every dollar put into arts and culture expenditure, there is a six-fold return, compared to dollars put into manufacturing, because such a high proportion of this funding comes back in salaries
April 16, 1985

and is returned to government in taxes and can be ploughed back for further investment. Money spent by government in arts and culture means good jobs for Canadians, which in turn improves the quality of life of Canadians.
In conclusion I would like to point out that the proposals which the NDP caucus has brought forward are very constructive. We have the evidence of other countries with social democratic governments, and of the Government of Manitoba which has instituted constructive proposals and job initiation funds with the result of lower unemployment and economic growth. We know it can be done. We are not talking about abstract theories. We are talking about realities where people and governments put jobs and building communities first. It can be done and we propose the measures to do it.

IMMIGRATION-COMMITTEE REPORT-ENTREPRENEURSHIP ADVOCACY. (B) CONSIDERATION OF REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the adjournment debate, following up on a question I asked on April 2 of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). The question dealt with the recent report of Conservative Members on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration which suggested that our immigration levels be increased in the coming years largely with immigrants who are entrepreneurs. In very simple, everyday language the recommendation suggested that immigration increases should only involve rich immigrants.
My question on April 2 was whether the Minister agreed with this premise and whether she was prepared to act on it, or whether she was prepared to replace that with a thorough and genuine parliamentary process in close concert with Canadians. At the time the Minister was not in the House. The Acting Minister got up, ranted and raved, but went around the issue quite nicely. I am hopeful that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister will provide some sense of leadership and given an answer to the question.
Adjournment Debate
My Party and I are certainly not opposed to having entrepreneurs consider Canada their new home. We encourage and support that. In fact, the entrepreneur stream within the immigration policy was instituted by this Party while it was in Government. However, we feel that rich immigrants should not be the cornerstone of an immigration policy. To embark on this path would be to turn back the clock on what has been the development of a progressive and compassionate policy within the context of a multicultural and multilingual Canada. That policy values the principle of family re-unification and the principle of assisting family streams so that Canadians can have the opportunity of sponsoring relatives and friends from abroad.
I would like to quote the recommendation which is really the essence of the report. It is Item 9 under Economic Considerations. It reads:
When the economic consideration is paramount in increasing the immigration level, then the fundamental principle should be the active recruitment of people who are either self-supporting, or who can clearly contribute to the growth of the Canadian economy. For example: those who fit current regulations for entrepreneurial immigration ... bring with them investment capital which they will use to create new jobs and export potential,... self-employed immigrants, etc. The current consultation process for 1986 should focus on ways to encourage, in every possible way, increasing the number of people whose immigration to Canada would enhance our economic capacity.
A recent article in The Toronto Star quoted the chairman of that Standing Committee who suggested that the ideal immigrant:
-should come from a developed nation, preferably the U.S. or one of the Western European countries-should have a good business background, equity capital in the neighbourhood of $500,000 and an impulse to create.
I am surprised that the chairman did not go further and propose that specifications on an individual's hair colour, weight and height be added to the list of criteria that he has outlined for this Parliament.
The essence of the matter is that the guts of this report completely overlooks the contributions that thousands upon thousands of poor and average income immigrants have made to this country, and that the Government is trying to suggest that if you do not happen to be rich then you have not or cannot contribute to the economic growth of this country. That premise is completely false. The premise is that thousands of immigrants, poor and average income immigrants, have contributed to this country and have taken jobs. They have become successful businessmen, and that will continue to be the case in future.
The direction is very worrisome but the process by which the directions were formulated are equally as worrisome, Mr. Speaker. There was not one single witness outside of employment and immigration employees to appear before the committee. There was not one ethno-cultural group invited, nor one immigrant aid society, nor one union, nor one professor, nor one economist. Nor was any economic study done on this question.

April 16, 1985

Mr. Speaker, even though I have here a prepared answer, I wish nevertheless to elaborate on the assertion that has just been made by my colleague. "The process is worrisome" .. . Well, the House of Commons has decided to set up committees to study specific problems and we have heard some witnesses. It should be said as well that there may have been more witnesses than opposition members during the committee sittings.
We have heard witnesses and we have never come to a conclusion, Mr. Speaker, whereby the policy of family reunification was set aside. This policy remains a priority, as well as the one concerning refugees. Immigration covers many aspects, it is a large area in which many possibilities are explored and we have decided, within that framework, to stress this particular aspect. This does not mean however that other areas are overlooked. Is the Minister going to answer? As you may see when you read the last paragraph of the report, the Minister has a number of days to give her reply. Why does the Hon. Member claim right now that the Minister has not answered since she has a few days to do it? We are trying to put the emphasis on one specific area in order to encourage entrepreneurs who will also create jobs to come to this country. This does not mean that we give up family reunification. It is recognized that they are consumers, as well as the people whom you call "regular or ordinary". It is widely recognized but we are allowed, as a committee, to stress one particular group which we would like to see coming to Canada in larger numbers.
This is the substance of the report and the Hon. Minister will table in the House, within the deadline provided in our Standing Orders, the report or the reply concerning those recommendations. But this report must be considered in its particular outlook. We were studying the case of entrepreneurs as we are now beginning to study that of refugees. When the committee studies and tables a report on refugees, it will not mean that entrepreneurs will be left aside. We must look at all possibilities within an immigration policy which the Minister undertook to review under the revision process and this is what committees are here for. We hear witnesses, we table a report, a reply will be forthcoming from the Department and in the meantime, we will continue to consider all other aspects.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS SUBSTANCES. (B) DEBATE ON LEGISLATION
REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS SUBSTANCES. (B) DEBATE ON LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a question I asked the Minister of
Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) today about a series of spills of PCBs which occurred just a few days ago between Thunder Bay and Kenora, eventually discovered when the truck in question pulled into a gas station in Kenora.
Before following up on my question, I should just like to say that this kind of incident was bound to happen. It was only a matter of time, really, before our collective negligence-and I say collective negligence because I am not trying to point the finger at anyone in particular-with respect to the transportation of dangerous goods caught up with us. This incident is a sign of those practices having caught up with us, as it happens to have occurred before the regulations, which are supposed to be in place as a result of the transportation of dangerous goods Bill, took effect.
One has to ask why it takes so long to get regulations in place. I ask that question not just of this Government but of all Governments. I certainly had the impression when we passed the transportation of dangerous goods legislation in the House a couple of years ago that certain things would come into effect and that people could breathe a little easier about the transportation of dangerous goods. However, that turns out not to be the case. I know there have been some regulations with respect to rail transportation, but the ones having to do with road transportation apparently have not come into effect. One just wonders why there cannot be a more speedy process when it comes to the regulations which follow legislation.
I put my question to the Minister in a very non-partisan and objective way about having a moratorium on any further shipments of these kinds of substances between now and July 1 when the new regulations will come into effect. The Minister responded by going into a tirade about the NDP wanting to see the regulations back when the Bill was passed. Then he brought up the question of the new aeronautics Bill. In all these cases we have not tried to prevent speedy passage of legislation. All we argue is that it would be nice if at the same time we were able to see the regulations. That is the substance of what is going on.
It would be nice if the House of Commons actually had the opportunity sometime to see what are the regulations that follow such legislation. I know the Hon. Member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has been of that opinion himself, having spent many years on the transport committee. It would be nice if Members of Parliament did not just have a set of principles in front of them, but actually something about which they could seek opinions with respect to effectiveness. That is all the NDP has ever argued for in that regard. I am sorry the Minister decided to be so defensive about it and did not answer the question whether we would consider a moratorium between now and July 1, although I took it from his answer that he would not consider it.
This brings up the larger question of how we as a society face up to the fact that we have created all this waste. Our way of life, particularly since the second world war, with increasing dependence on synthetic substances, for instance, has created mountains of waste which we now do not know what to do with. Sooner or later we will have to face up to the
April 16, 1985

fact that in our way of life, or in our way of doing things, whether for profit, convenience, efficiency or whatever, we have in a way sown the wind and reaped the whirlwind. We are reaping the whirlwind now in that we have this manifold list of problems we have to deal with, whether it is toxic wastes in the Great Lakes, the transportation of PCBs, acid rain or whatever. These are just a few examples-perhaps the ones which have been given more attention-of the ways in which our way of life is catching up with us. We have to face difficult questions about whether we continue, even with regulations, to transport these dangerous wastes from one province to another, across the country from Ontario or Quebec to Alberta, or whether we opt for the option of having indigenous waste disposal. That is to say having it happen on a province by province basis so that we do not subject areas in between to the risks that will inevitably remain, in spite of whatever kind of regulations we adopt.
It is clear that we need to reduce our dependence on these substances. This will not help with respect to PCBs. PCBs have already been banned. It is just a question of dealing with the PCBs we already have. There are many other substances which are continually coming into existence as a result of technological and scientific innovation. We will only find out years from now the environmental effects. We need to ask ourselves whether we want to become even more dependent on these kinds of substances, or whether we want to begin to find ways of lessening this dependence. That is the direction we ought to go. Instead of looking for the next technological fix, we ought to be considering ways of using more natural substances, substances which do not pose the dangers that these pose.
Finally, I might say to the Government that it would find there would be a great deal of public support for this. It is one of the tragedies of the cuts that have taken place with respect to the environment. People are willing to support government spending when it comes to environmental protection. They do not want to see cut-backs in that area. There are plenty of things they would like to see cut, but environmental protection is not one of them. If this Government could sense that and go ahead and spend whatever it has to spend and do whatever it has to do face up to the problem of interprovincial transport of dangerous goods-acid rain, toxic wastes in the Great Lakes or wherever it happens to be-it would find there would be no public outcry whatsoever. Instead, there would be a collective sigh of relief that we finally have a Government that is not afraid to spend that kind of money and do what is needed to be done.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: REQUEST FOR MORATORIUM ON TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS SUBSTANCES. (B) DEBATE ON LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome and of course share the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member with respect to this matter. I must advise him that it is simply not within the power of the federal Government alone to accede to the recommendation he puts forward. Such a sweeping prohibition
Adjournment Debate
is simply not within the federal Government's capacity alone to effect.
Transportation of dangerous goods is a complex subject involving the interests of federal, provincial and municipal authorities. It involves a variety of authorities at all levels. It involves the necessity of the federal, provincial and municipal Governments acting in concert. To act in concert there must be a rationalized, harmonious compilation of all of the existing regulations that are dedicated to the very fair proposition the Member has put forward. It is fair in the sense of the concern that all Canadians have. It is a concern that the residents of the Kenora River area have had in the last day or two and will have until the formal investigation is completed, the results are known and the follow-up work and acitivities can take place. The regulations we are dealing with pick up the responsibility that we must face to industry and to society in general.
I have to use the term impassioned plea, but I understand from whence it came. On the other hand, were we to ban all such movements, what about gasoline trucks and chlorine for our water systems? Would the Hon. Member have us put a moratorium on all of those until such time as the regulations come into effect on July 1 ? Is that what he is suggesting? His question tended to imply that. We move some 200 million tonnes of chemicals annually in this country. We cannot simply interrupt that because of the impact it would have on society in general.
The Government has indicated that it is taking measured responses to this accident. An investigation is being conducted jointly by Transport Canada and appropriate provincial Government staff into the circumstances of the leakage, and this can be done now that the emergency response actions are concluded or nearly concluded.
On the basis of that investigation, appropriate, specific and deliberate considered actions will be taken to reduce the probability of such an accident in the future. I trust the Hon. Member will accept this as a partial response, and accept as well the Minister's concern and, I am sure the concern of all those involved.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PRICE OF WINTER WHEAT
CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PRICE OF WINTER WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address my comments on the Adjournment Debate tonight to the Canadian Wheat Board. My comments follow a question I asked earlier regarding winter wheat production, particularly the pricing pool in which winter wheat presently operates along with spring wheat.
By way of background, in my home Province of Saskatchewan winter wheat has enjoyed a particular popularity of late. As recently as 1983 there were 150,000 acres seeded to winter wheat. The next year, 1984, that figure had more than doubled to 350,000 acres seeded to winter wheat. By the time the 1985 winter wheat harvest is off, within the next two months, it

April 16, 1985
Adjournment Debate
should have exceeded about one million acres for this crop year.
Many farmers who in the past five or 10 years have begun growing winter wheat have the concern that, due to the unique nature of their wheat and its growing popularity, it should be put in its own separate pricing pool within the Canadian Wheat Board pricing system. They request this on the basis of their belief that in presently sharing the system with spring wheat they are subsidizing the price of spring wheat due to the export position of winter wheat. One young farmer has written to me indicating that he feels as a winter wheat producer that he is subsidizing spring wheat producers to the extent of $ 1 per bushel. I know that the Canadian Wheat Board has stated on many occasions that, with the varieties of grain it is marketing and selling abroad, it does not like to have in one pricing pool the cross-subsidization of one kind of grain with another.
Winter wheat is being sold and has been sold in the past few years primarily to the eastern area of our world, including China and India. The relatively good proximity of western Canada to the Port of Vancouver and the ease with which we can move winter wheat to the eastern countries that have expressed an interest in it further backs up the concern of farmers that by selling their product in the same pricing pool as spring wheat they may not in fact be getting the best independent price for their product.
To look further at the effect winter wheat has had on the growing patterns of Saskatchewan farmers, we should consider the increase of late in bushels of winter wheat grown. In 1984, in the Province of Saskatchewan alone, farmers produced nine million bushels of winter wheat. With many more farmers entertaining the thought of beginning to grow winter wheat, and with the farmers who are now doing so, it is my thought as their Member of Parliament that the Canadian Wheat Board ought first of all to address the question of whether or not winter wheat should be put in its own pricing pool and, second, do this with an eye to the present market and the present timing.
Winter wheat by its very nature is seeded in the fall and harvested in the spring. The winter wheat harvest will be occurring in Saskatchewan within the next couple of months, and producers who have this concern are interested in seeing if the Canadian Wheat Board will give some consideration to this matter, if it will consider the implementation of any program, keeping in mind that the harvest will soon be off and the producers will then be looking to sell their product through the Canadian Wheat Board. It is a good time to ask the Canadian Wheat Board to consider this matter expeditiously. If action is to be taken, it should be done soon.
I would like to conclude my remarks in further support of the many farmers in my constituency who have been growing winter wheat over the past winter. They have only started in the past two or three years to begin actively growing winter wheat. Generally, winter cereals have been one reason for example, within the European Economic Community, why the
British farmer has had an incredible turnaround during the past ten years. Britain was a very heavy importer of Canadian grain. It is now a world exporter of grain. Through winter cereals, such as winter wheat, the British farmers found that they can have a good yield wheat if winter conditions are favourable for growing. I would ask the Canadian Wheat Board to give this matter further consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PRICE OF WINTER WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for The Batt-lefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) has raised a very interesting question. Indeed it is true that the acreage planted with winter wheat in Alberta and Saskatchewan has increased substantially in recent years. In 1981, 300,00 acres were planted and we already have 1,750,000 acres in 1985, which is quite considerable. Even in Alberta, as well as in Saskatchewan, the acreage planted has increased quite substantially.
The problem may not lie strictly at this level as it is only for the past eleven years that red winter wheat exports have never exceeded the high of 269,000 which had been reached in 1981-82. The following year, exports fell to 129,000 tons, but they again increased to 258,000 tons in 1983-84.
In fact, last year, these exports accounted for only 1.4 per cent of total Canadian wheat exports. In 1983-84, all red winter wheat exports were shipped to two markets, India and China. The previous year, all our exports went to China, while, in the years before that, they went to a greater number of markets. However, in the six or seven years previous, 60 per cent of the winter wheat had always been exported through CIDA, which purchased the wheat and shipped it to the various countries receiving Canadian food assistance.
Mr. Speaker-

This export profile will be cause for concern in considering a separate pool for red winter wheat. The dependence on a few markets for exports of red winter wheat could present a risk that a separate pool may be more exposed to the requirements of a few countries. Especially important to bear in mind would be the risk that with the larger production of red winter wheat which can be expected in 1985, finding markets for these larger quantities may be more difficult than finding markets for the smaller quantities of past years, particularly as they would be marketed mainly in competition with U.S. red winter, which is their major class of wheat. In view of such uncertainties, the producers of winter wheat may welcome the benefits of pooling all wheat other than Durum in a single pool until such time as the experience with larger quantities of winter wheat is adequate to judge whether it would be advantageous to have a separate pool.

April 16, 1985
